adjudications.title: C4: do SR12 + SR24 together forbid a REPEATED IS-form character-1 in one picture string?

first.fork: C4-fork2-SR12-SR24-repeated-IS — do §13.18.40.3 SR12 + SR24, read together, forbid a REPEATED IS-form character-1 in one picture string (i.e. is `PIC 9G9G9 EDITING "G" IS "<>"` illegal)?
first.classification: SPEC-RESOLVED (resolved AGAINST the prohibition — repetition is legal). The fork's premise, that the IS form falls inside SR24's scope, is defeated by §13.18.40.5 editing rule 3.

governingText.section: §13.18.40.5, Editing rules, rule 3 (Simple insertion editing) — spec line 20768
governingText.quote: Character-1 and the symbols 'B', '0', '/', ',' and, if literal=1 is specified, character-1 are used as the simple insertion editing symbols.
governingText.bearing: DECISIVE. The IS form (literal-1 specified) makes character-1 a SIMPLE INSERTION editing symbol, not a fixed-insertion sign symbol. SR24's first sentence is scoped 'For fixed insertion with editing sign control symbols' and therefore never reaches it. Simple insertion symbols ('B','0','/',',') are freely repeatable; character-1 under IS is enumerated in that same set.

governingText.section: §13.18.40.5, Editing rules, rule 5 (Fixed insertion editing) — spec line 20784
governingText.quote: When character-1 is used, and is not a simple insertion character, it represents literal-2, or literal-3 as the insertion characters.
governingText.bearing: Confirms the partition: in FIXED insertion, character-1 only ever carries literal-2/literal-3 (the FOR form). By negation, character-1 carrying literal-1 is a simple insertion character. This resolves the looseness in GR14 'es' ('simple insertion symbol or a fixed insertion symbol').

governingText.section: §13.18.40.5, Table 8 — Results of fixed insertion editing (spec line 20796)
governingText.quote:
| character-1, NEGATIVE phrase | literal-2 | literal-2 or spaces |
| character-1, POSITIVE phrase | literal-3 or spaces | literal-3 |
governingText.bearing: The operative table for fixed-insertion sign results has rows ONLY for the FOR form. There is no row producing a sign-dependent result for a literal-1 character-1 — the IS form has no sign-control behavior at all, so labelling it a 'sign control symbol' is inert.

governingText.section: §13.18.40.3 SR12, non-FOR branch, sub-rule a) — spec lines 20309–20317
governingText.quote: If the FOR phrase is not specified, the following rules apply: a) Character-string-1 shall contain: — at least on[e] one of the symbols from the set 'A', 'N', 'X', 'Z', '1', '9', *, or — at least two occurrences of one of the symbols from the set character-1, 'x', '+', '-', and the currency symbol.
governingText.bearing: SR12's OWN non-FOR branch (the branch the IS form lives in) expressly contemplates 'at least two occurrences of ... character-1' as a validity criterion. SR12 cannot be read as forbidding what its own sub-rule uses as a legality test.

governingText.quote: If the EDITING phrase is specified, the character identified by character-1 shall appear at least once in character-string-1.
governingText.bearing: 'At least once' is a floor, not a cap. The drafters wrote a minimum-occurrence rule and no corresponding maximum for the IS form.

governingText.quote: If more than one EDITING phrase is specified in one PICTURE clause, no two instances of character-1 shall be the same character.
governingText.bearing: The only uniqueness rule in the EDITING family constrains character-1 ACROSS phrases, not occurrences of one character-1 WITHIN character-string-1. Expressio unius: the drafters knew how to write a distinctness rule and scoped it elsewhere.

governingText.quote: For fixed insertion with editing sign control symbols, only one currency symbol and only one editing sign control symbol may be used in character-string-1. For extended editing sign control symbols, either one or two extended editing sign control symbols may be used in character-string-1.
governingText.bearing: The rule under test. Sentence 1 is scoped to FIXED INSERTION; 'editing sign control symbols' is the defined set '+','-','CR','DB' (SR23, GR14). Sentence 2 handles the FOR form under its own coined term. Neither sentence has any subject that is the IS form once editing rule 3 classes it as simple insertion.

governingText.quote: The editing sign control symbols '+', '-', 'CR', and 'DB' are mutually exclusive in character-string-1 ...
governingText.bearing: Fixes the extension of the term 'editing sign control symbols' used unqualified in SR24 sentence 1 to the four built-in symbols.

governingText.quote: If literal-1 is specified, character-1 is a fixed editing sign control symbol.
governingText.bearing: The sentence that generates the apparent conflict. It is contradicted by editing rule 3, editing rule 5, Table 8, GR7/GR10 and Annex E.3.3 item 19 — a drafting defect (it should read 'simple insertion symbol', or 'fixed' means fixed-POSITION as opposed to floating). It is a labelling sentence with no behavioral consequence anywhere in the standard.

governingText.section: §13.18.40.4 GR7 and GR10 — spec lines ~20500 (alphanumeric-edited / national-edited)
governingText.quote: To define an item as alphanumeric-edited, character-string-1 shall include — at least one symbol 'A' or one symbol 'X', and — at least one instance of character-1 or one of the symbols from the set 'B', '0', '/'.
governingText.bearing: Character-1 is grouped with the simple insertion symbols B/0//. Table 7 permits ONLY simple insertion for alphanumeric-edited and national-edited items. Under the literal SR12 reading (character-1 = a sign control symbol) an IS-form character-1 could never legally occur in an alphanumeric-edited item, contradicting GR7/GR10 outright.

governingText.section: §13.18.40.5 Table 7 — Category and type of editing (spec line ~20745)
governingText.quote:
| Alphanumeric-edited | Simple insertion |
| National-edited | Simple insertion |
governingText.bearing: Seals the GR7/GR10 argument: character-1 in those categories must be a simple insertion symbol, which is only possible via the IS (or bare) form.

governingText.quote: Character-1 in character-string-1 represents a character position into which the associated literal-1, literal-2, or literal-3 is to be placed. If character-1 is a simple insertion symbol or a fixed insertion symbol, the size of literal-1 is counted in the size of the item.
governingText.bearing: The size rule for the IS form is stated PER OCCURRENCE ('a character position ... into which'), and it is the simple/fixed-insertion clause — separate from the very next sentence about 'fixed editing sign control symbols'. Gives the sizing rule for a repeated IS-form character-1.

governingText.quote: If the FOR clause is not specified, the character position (s) corresponding to character-1 shall be checked to contain literal-1.
governingText.bearing: Plural 'position(s)' for the non-FOR form, each checked to contain literal-1 — the VALIDATE-side rule already presumes possibly-multiple occurrences and specifies a per-occurrence, sign-independent check.

governingText.quote: EDITING phrase. The EDITING phrase of the PICTURE clause adds the capability to specify a literal of any size for simple insertion and sign-sensitive fixed insertion.
governingText.bearing: The change-list statement of intent names exactly two capabilities matching the two inner options: IS literal-1 = SIMPLE INSERTION; FOR = sign-sensitive fixed insertion. Independent confirmation that SR12's first sentence is mislabelled.

governingText.quote: If the EDITING phrase is specified, the precedence of 'es' as related to Table 10, Format 1 picture symbol order of precedence, has the same precedence as the 'cs' symbol in the column and row of non-floating insertion symbols.
governingText.bearing: The ONLY residual counter-signal. Non-floating 'cs' has no x at its own row/column intersection (single occurrence), so a mechanical borrow would forbid es-after-es. Defeated by: (i) the borrow is an ORDER-of-precedence statement ('may precede ... in character-string-1'), and cs's two rows/columns encode alternative POSITIONS (leftmost vs rightmost), not a count — the count cap on cs comes from SR24, a rule whose scope excludes the IS form; (ii) §13.18.40.6's own preamble makes further restriction flow FROM syntax rules, and SR12a affirmatively permits two occurrences; (iii) under editing rule 3 the IS form is a simple insertion symbol, whose row/column self-intersection IS 'x'.

governingText.quote: Where an 'x' appears in Table 10 and in Table 11, additional syntax rules or general rules may apply further restrictions.
governingText.bearing: Establishes the direction of authority: the table is refined by the syntax/general rules. It does not authorize inventing a prohibition the syntax rules do not state.

governingText.section: Annex D.24 — Examples of the use of the EDITING phrase (spec lines 48133–48179)
governingText.quote:
01 item PIC IS LLLL9.99F
   EDITING "L" FOR NEGATIVE IS "("
   EDITING "F" FOR NEGATIVE IS ")"
   BLANK WHEN ZERO.  ... would result in 'b(123.45)' ... 'PIC LLLL9,88 EDITING "L" FOR NEGATIVE IS "DEBIT "' would result in an item size of 13 characters: 6 for the first 'L', 3 for the next three, and 4 for the numbers.
governingText.bearing: REPORTED HONESTLY: D.24 contains FOUR examples and ALL FOUR use the FOR form. There is NO IS-form example anywhere in D.24, so D.24 does NOT directly settle the IS-form question. What it does settle collaterally: repeated character-1 is unambiguously legal in the standard (LLLL, four occurrences), and SR24's 'either one or two extended editing sign control symbols' counts EDITING-phrase SYMBOLS (L, F = two), not raw character occurrences — so SR24's counting idiom is per-symbol, not per-occurrence, which independently blunts the fork's reading even if SR24 did reach the IS form.

first.derivation:
1. The fork's syllogism is: SR12 says the IS form is a "fixed editing sign control symbol"; SR24 says "only one editing sign control symbol may be used in character-string-1"; therefore repetition is illegal. The chain breaks at both links.

2. LINK 1 BREAKS — SR24's scope. SR24 sentence 1 is expressly conditioned: "For fixed insertion with editing sign control symbols…". §13.18.40.5 editing rule 3 places the IS form squarely in SIMPLE insertion: "Character-1 and the symbols 'B', '0', '/', ',' and, if literal-1 is specified, character-1 are used as the simple insertion editing symbols." Editing rule 5 confirms the partition from the other side: in fixed insertion, "When character-1 is used, and is not a simple insertion character, it represents literal-2, or literal-3" — i.e. fixed-insertion character-1 is always the FOR form. The IS form is therefore not "fixed insertion", and SR24 sentence 1 has no application to it. SR24 sentence 2 is expressly about "extended editing sign control symbols", SR12's coined term for the FOR form. Neither sentence has the IS form as its subject.

3. LINK 2 BREAKS — SR12's label is inert and defective. Nothing in the standard attaches behavior to the phrase "fixed editing sign control symbol" as applied to a literal-1 character-1: Table 8 (the operative results table for fixed insertion sign editing) has rows only for "character-1, NEGATIVE phrase" and "character-1, POSITIVE phrase", i.e. only the FOR form; the IS form produces literal-1 unconditionally regardless of sign, which is by definition not sign control. Annex E.3.3 item 19 states the feature's intent as "a literal of any size for simple insertion and sign-sensitive fixed insertion" — two capabilities, matching the two inner syntax options, with IS = simple insertion. GR15's validation rule for the non-FOR case is likewise sign-independent. SR12 sentence 1 is a drafting slip (or "fixed" means fixed-position, i.e. non-floating); either way it carries no operative consequence that SR24 could amplify.

4. REDUCTIO. If SR12 sentence 1 were read literally as the fork proposes, GR7 and GR10 become unsatisfiable in part: they define alphanumeric-edited and national-edited items as containing "at least one instance of character-1 or one of the symbols from the set 'B', '0', '/'", while Table 7 permits ONLY simple insertion for those categories. A character-1 that were categorically a sign control symbol could never appear there. The literal reading contradicts the general rules; the editing-rule-3 reading harmonizes them.

5. AFFIRMATIVE PERMISSION. SR10 sets a floor only ("shall appear at least once"). SR11 scopes distinctness across EDITING phrases, not within character-string-1 — the drafters wrote a uniqueness rule and deliberately did not aim it here. Most directly, SR12's own non-FOR branch sub-rule a) makes "at least two occurrences of one of the symbols from the set character-1, 'x', '+', '-', and the currency symbol" a sufficient condition for character-string-1's validity. SR12 therefore affirmatively contemplates two-or-more occurrences of character-1 in exactly the branch the IS form inhabits. A rule cannot forbid what its own sub-rule uses as a legality test.

6. THE ONE RESIDUAL COUNTER-SIGNAL, addressed. §13.18.40.6's closing note borrows non-floating 'cs' precedence for 'es'. Non-floating cs has no self-intersection 'x' in Table 10, so a mechanical borrow would bar es-after-es. This does not survive: (a) the borrow is about ORDER ("may precede … in character-string-1"), and cs's duplicated row/column encodes leftmost-vs-rightmost POSITION, not multiplicity — the single-cs cap is imposed by SR24, whose scope we have shown excludes the IS form, so borrowing cs's precedence does not import SR24's cap; (b) §13.18.40.6's preamble routes further restriction through the syntax/general rules, and SR12a affirmatively permits two occurrences, so the tables cannot be used to manufacture a prohibition the rules deny; (c) once editing rule 3 classes the IS form as a simple insertion symbol, the natural precedence for it is the B/0// row, whose self-intersection is 'x'. The borrow is best read as governing the non-floating FIXED-insertion (FOR) use of 'es', which is where a cs-like leftmost/rightmost discipline is actually needed (see SR25 and SR26, which do exactly that).

7. ANNEX D.24, reported exactly. D.24 has four examples: L9999.99F, LLLL9.99F, L999.99, and the sizing discussion of LLLL9,88 — every one uses `FOR NEGATIVE IS`. There is NO `IS literal-1` example in D.24 at all. So D.24 does not directly settle the IS-form question and must not be cited as if it did. It does supply two collateral facts: repeated character-1 (LLLL) is beyond doubt legal in the standard, and SR24's "either one or two extended editing sign control symbols" counts EDITING-phrase symbols (L and F = two) rather than character occurrences (four L's) — meaning even a fork-favorable reading of SR24's scope would not convert repeated occurrences into "more than one symbol".
first.annexEvidence: Annex D.24 (spec lines 48133–48179) contains FOUR examples and every one uses the FOR form (`EDITING "L" FOR NEGATIVE IS "("`, `EDITING "F" FOR NEGATIVE IS ")"`, `EDITING "L" FOR NEGATIVE IS "DEBIT "`). It shows NO `IS literal-1` example whatsoever, so it does not directly settle the IS-form repetition question — this must be stated plainly rather than papered over. It settles two adjacent points: (1) repeated character-1 is unquestionably legal in the standard — `PIC IS LLLL9.99F` yields 'b(123.45)' and `PIC LLLL9,88` is analysed as "an item size of 13 characters: 6 for the first 'L', 3 for the next three, and 4 for the numbers"; (2) SR24's "one or two" counts EDITING-phrase symbols (L, F), not character occurrences (four L's) — a per-symbol counting idiom that would not turn `9G9G9` into "two symbols" even if SR24 reached the IS form. Annex E.3.3 item 19 (line 50275) is the stronger annex evidence: "The EDITING phrase of the PICTURE clause adds the capability to specify a literal of any size for simple insertion and sign-sensitive fixed insertion" — two capabilities for the two inner options, confirming IS = simple insertion and exposing SR12 sentence 1 as mislabelled. Annex F (obsolete elements) has no bearing; the EDITING phrase is new in 2023 (E.2 item 25 reserves the word EDITING at 2023), so there is no prior-edition behavior to reconcile and docs/VERSION_CHANGE_REFERENCE.md row 62 correctly records it as a 2014→2023 addition with no cross-edition variance.
first.answer:
SPEC-RESOLVED, and resolved AGAINST the prohibition. SR12 and SR24 do NOT forbid a repeated IS-form character-1. `PIC 9G9G9 EDITING "G" IS "<>"` is LEGAL.

The single sentence that resolves it is §13.18.40.5, Editing rules, rule 3 (spec line 20768): "Character-1 and the symbols 'B', '0', '/', ',' and, if literal-1 is specified, character-1 are used as the simple insertion editing symbols." SR24's first sentence is scoped "For fixed insertion with editing sign control symbols"; the IS form is simple insertion, so SR24 never reaches it. Editing rule 5 confirms the partition from the other direction ("When character-1 is used, and is not a simple insertion character, it represents literal-2, or literal-3"), and Table 8 has no result row for a literal-1 character-1 — the IS form has no sign-control behavior at all.

Backstop if anyone disputes rule 3: SR12's OWN non-FOR branch, sub-rule a), makes "at least two occurrences of one of the symbols from the set character-1, 'x', '+', '-', and the currency symbol" a sufficient validity condition for character-string-1. SR12 affirmatively contemplates repeated character-1 in the IS branch. SR10 sets only a floor ("at least once") and SR11 scopes distinctness across EDITING phrases, not within the picture string.

SR12's first sentence ("If literal-1 is specified, character-1 is a fixed editing sign control symbol") is a drafting defect — or "fixed" means fixed-POSITION as opposed to floating. It is contradicted by editing rules 3 and 5, Table 8, GR7/GR10 read with Table 7 (alphanumeric-edited and national-edited permit ONLY simple insertion yet expressly admit character-1), GR15's sign-independent validation of the non-FOR case, and Annex E.3.3 item 19's statement of intent. Implement the behavior, not the label.

The C4 design's conclusion (exempt the IS form from SR24) is CORRECT but was recorded with the wrong justification. It should not be framed as an "exemption from SR24" — that framing concedes the IS form is in SR24's scope and then carves it out, which is exactly what has no textual basis. Re-base it: SR24 never applied, because editing rule 3 classifies the IS form as simple insertion. Cite §13.18.40.5 rule 3 (line 20768) as primary, SR12a (lines 20309–20317) as corroborating.

Honest caveat, recorded rather than suppressed: one sentence cuts the other way — §13.18.40.6's closing note (line 21010) borrows non-floating 'cs' precedence for 'es', and non-floating cs has no self-intersection in Table 10. I judge this insufficient to create a genuine fork, for three reasons given in the derivation (the borrow is about ORDER not COUNT; cs's single-occurrence cap comes from SR24 whose scope excludes the IS form, so it is not imported with the precedence; and §13.18.40.6's preamble routes further restriction through the syntax rules, where SR12a affirmatively permits two occurrences). This does NOT warrant an owner decision. If a future conformance-suite conflict ever surfaces on it, that note is the place to look.

Annex D.24 does NOT settle this question and must not be cited as if it did: all four of its examples use the FOR form and it contains no `IS literal-1` example at all.
first.implementationConsequence:
PictureAnalyzer / the EDITING validation path:

1. DO NOT enforce SR24's "only one editing sign control symbol" against an IS-form (literal-1) character-1. SR24 sentence 1 applies only to the built-in fixed-insertion sign symbols '+', '-', 'CR', 'DB' (per SR23/GR14) plus the one-currency-symbol cap. SR24 sentence 2 (one or two) applies only to the FOR form (extended editing sign control symbols), and counts EDITING-PHRASE SYMBOLS, not character occurrences — D.24's `LLLL9.99F` is two symbols (L, F), not five. The existing scout note in docs/rearchitecture/PHASE-13-remaining-waves-scout.md line 71, which says "char-1 appearing exactly once (fixed, per SR24)", is correct only for the FOR/non-floating case and must not be generalized to the IS form; docs/rearchitecture/PHASE-13-wave-c-scout.md line 285 already has the right two-mode split.

2. ALLOW N occurrences (N >= 1) of an IS-form character-1 anywhere the precedence table admits a simple insertion symbol. Treat IS-form 'es' as a member of the simple insertion class alongside 'B', '0', '/', ',' for both precedence checking and category determination. Enforce only SR10 (>= 1 occurrence) and SR11 (distinct character-1 across EDITING phrases).

3. SIZING (§13.18.40.4 GR14 'es'): each occurrence contributes len(literal-1) character positions. `PIC 9G9G9 EDITING "G" IS "<>"` has size 3 + 2*2 = 7. This is per-occurrence, unlike the currency symbol's first-occurrence-then-one-each rule — do not copy the cs sizing rule across with the precedence borrow.

4. EDITING SEMANTICS (§13.18.40.5 rule 3): each occurrence inserts literal-1 verbatim at the corresponding position, unconditionally and independent of the sign of the value. No Table 8 lookup, no sign branch. `MOVE 123 TO item` with the picture above yields `1<>2<>3`.

5. CATEGORY DETERMINATION: GR7/GR10 — an IS-form character-1 counts as a simple insertion instance for alphanumeric-edited and national-edited, so `PIC XGXGX EDITING "G" IS "<>"` is a valid alphanumeric-edited item (the exact analogue of `XBXBX`). GR13a — for numeric-edited, character-1 satisfies the "at least one symbol '9' and at least one instance of character-1" limb.

6. VALIDATE (GR15 'es'): for the non-FOR form, each character position group corresponding to an occurrence of character-1 is checked to contain literal-1 — per occurrence, sign-independent.

7. Keep enforcing, unchanged: SR8 (character-1 domain), SR9 (literal <= 50, national iff USAGE NATIONAL or 'N'), SR12a (literal-2/literal-3 equal width), SR12b (FOR ⇒ mask ⊆ {character-1, '9', '.', cs, 'P', 'V', 'Z'}), SR12c (unspecified sign defaults to spaces of the specified literal's width), SR12 last-a (no extended sign control on a floating-point edited item), SR25/SR26 (two-extended ordering and currency adjacency). None of these are touched by this adjudication.

8. TESTS (per feedback_conformance_tests_per_feature, same commit): positive golden for `PIC 9G9G9 EDITING "G" IS "<>"` → size 7, `MOVE 123` → `1<>2<>3`; positive golden for the alphanumeric-edited analogue `PIC XGXGX`; and a negative golden asserting SR24 STILL fires for the genuine cases (two built-in sign symbols; three extended sign symbols) so the narrowed scope is pinned in both directions and cannot silently widen.

9. DOC UPDATE (same change set, per process rule 4): amend the C4 design's IS-form note to cite §13.18.40.5 rule 3 (line 20768) + SR12a as the basis, and to state explicitly that SR24 never applied — replacing the current uncited "exemption from SR24" framing, which concedes the wrong premise. Record the §13.18.40.6 line-21010 'es'/'cs' precedence-borrow caveat as a known-and-considered residual, with the three reasons it does not control, so a future reader does not re-litigate it from scratch.
first.confidence:
HIGH that the answer is "repetition is legal" and that this needs no owner decision. Five independent lines of text converge: editing rule 3 (direct classification), editing rule 5 (the partition from the other side), Table 8 (no sign-control row exists for the IS form), GR7/GR10 with Table 7 (the literal reading is unsatisfiable there), and SR12's own sub-rule a) (affirmative permission for two occurrences). Annex E.3.3 item 19 independently confirms the IS/FOR = simple/fixed-sign split. Convergence this broad against a single mislabelling sentence is not a close call.

MEDIUM-HIGH specifically on the §13.18.40.6 line-21010 precedence-borrow point — that sentence is loosely drafted (it says "the column and row" singular though non-floating cs occupies two of each) and a mechanical reading of it would bar es-after-es. I resolve it against the fork on the grounds set out above, but I am flagging it rather than burying it: it is the one place a conformance-suite disagreement could plausibly surface, and if it ever does, that is a defect-report question for the standards committee, not a design fork for the owner.

Stated for the record: I looked for a genuine fork here and did not find one. SR12's first sentence is real textual friction, but friction that five other rules resolve in one direction is a drafting defect, not an interpretive fork, and it should not consume an owner decision.

governingText.section: §13.18.40.5, Editing rules, rule 3 (Simple insertion editing) — line 20768
governingText.quote: Character-1 and the symbols 'B', '0', '/', ',' and, if literal=1 is specified, character-1 are used as the simple insertion editing symbols.
governingText.bearing: VERIFIED VERBATIM (including the 'literal=1' OCR artifact for 'literal-1'). The IS form makes character-1 a SIMPLE insertion editing symbol. Note the sentence names character-1 twice — a drafting/OCR redundancy — but the operative conditional clause is unambiguous.

governingText.section: §13.18.40.5, Editing rules, rule 5 (Fixed insertion editing), FIRST sentence — line ~20780 [OMITTED FROM THE PACKET]
governingText.quote: Character-1, the currency symbol and the editing sign control symbols '+', '-', 'CR' and 'DB' are used as the fixed insertion editing symbols.
governingText.bearing: THE STRONGEST PRO-FORK TEXT, and the packet did not quote it. Character-1 appears in the fixed-insertion symbol list too. Standing alone this would put character-1 inside SR24's 'fixed insertion' scope. It is neutralized only by rule 5's third sentence — which means the partition, not rule 3 alone, is what resolves the fork.

governingText.section: §13.18.40.5, Editing rules, rule 5, THIRD sentence — line 20784
governingText.quote: When character-1 is used, and is not a simple insertion character, it represents literal-2, or literal-3 as the insertion characters.
governingText.bearing: The actual disambiguator. The qualifier 'and is not a simple insertion character' concedes that character-1 can be either, and confines its FIXED-insertion role to literal-2/literal-3 — i.e. the FOR form exclusively. Rules 3 and 5 together partition character-1: IS ⇒ simple, FOR ⇒ fixed.

governingText.quote: Character-1 in character-string-1 represents a character position into which the associated literal-1, literal-2, or literal-3 is to be placed. If character-1 is a simple insertion symbol or a fixed insertion symbol, the size of literal-1 is counted in the size of the item. For fixed editing sign control symbols, each character used in the symbol is counted in the size of the item. For extended editing sign control symbols with fixed insertion, each occurrence of the character(s) specified in the associated literal are counted in the size of the item. For floating inserting, one occurrence of literal-2 or literal-3 is counted in the size of the item plus one character for each repetition of character-1.
governingText.bearing: STRONGER THAN THE PACKET'S USE OF IT, and decisive on terminology. Sentence 3 — 'For fixed editing sign control symbols, each CHARACTER USED IN THE SYMBOL is counted' — can only denote '+','-','CR','DB' (CR/DB being two-character symbols). It cannot denote an IS-form character-1, whose literal-1 sizing was already disposed of by sentence 2. Therefore the General Rules use the term 'fixed editing sign control symbols' to mean the four built-ins, NOT the IS-form character-1 that SR12 labels with that phrase. SR24's subject is thus the built-ins.

governingText.quote: The editing sign control symbols '+', '-', 'CR', and 'DB' are mutually exclusive in character-string-1 with the exception of a numeric-edited data item for a floating-point edited result as described in General rule 13b.
governingText.bearing: Fixes the extension of 'editing sign control symbols' as used unqualified in SR24 sentence 1 to the four built-ins. Confirmed verbatim.

governingText.quote: For fixed insertion with editing sign control symbols, only one currency symbol and only one editing sign control symbol may be used in character-string-1. For extended editing sign control symbols, either one or two extended editing sign control symbols may be used in character-string-1.
governingText.bearing: The rule under test, confirmed verbatim. Sentence 1's subject, per SR23 + GR14 sentence 3, is '+','-','CR','DB' plus the currency symbol. Sentence 2's subject is the FOR form. Neither reaches an IS-form character-1.

governingText.section: §13.18.40.3 SR25 — lines ~20358–20362 [NOT CITED BY THE PACKET]

second.derivation:
I attempted to refute the adjudication and could not. I did find one material omission and two arguments that needed replacing with better text.

1. THE OMISSION. The packet quoted editing rule 5's THIRD sentence but not its FIRST: "Character-1, the currency symbol and the editing sign control symbols '+', '-', 'CR' and 'DB' are used as the fixed insertion editing symbols." That is the single best piece of text FOR the fork, and it was left out. This matters methodologically: the packet framed rule 3 as a clean one-sentence classification ("the IS form IS simple insertion, full stop"), when in fact character-1 appears in BOTH the simple-insertion list (rule 3) and the fixed-insertion list (rule 5). Rule 3 alone is therefore NOT decisive, contrary to the packet's headline claim. What is decisive is the PARTITION: rule 5's qualifier "and is not a simple insertion character" concedes character-1 can be either, and assigns its fixed-insertion role exclusively to literal-2/literal-3 — the FOR form. The conclusion survives; the stated ground does not, and should be corrected before it is written into a design doc.

2. TERMINOLOGY — a stronger kill than the packet found. The packet treated SR12 sentence 1 as a "drafting defect", which is an uncomfortable position (implementors should not need to declare the standard wrong). There is a cleaner route. GR14's 'es' entry uses the very phrase SR24 uses: "For fixed editing sign control symbols, each character used in the symbol is counted in the size of the item." "Each character used in the symbol" can only mean '+','-','CR','DB' — CR and DB being the two-character symbols that sentence exists to size. It cannot mean an IS-form character-1, because the immediately preceding sentence already sized literal-1. So the General Rules demonstrably use "fixed editing sign control symbols" to denote the built-ins. SR24 sentence 1 uses the same term. SR12's sentence 1 applies that label to something the operative rules never treat as such — so it is a term-of-art collision, not a rule with which SR24 must be reconciled. No defect declaration required.

3. COUNTING — the packet's weakest argument, replaceable. The packet inferred from Annex D.24 that SR24's "one or two" counts EDITING-phrase symbols rather than character occurrences. That inference is sound but indirect, and D.24 is informative. SR25 states it NORMATIVELY: "When extended editing sign control symbols are used and two are specified, the first occurrence of the EDITING PHRASE shall be for the leftmost symbol ... and the second occurrence shall be for the rightmost." SR24's unit of count is the EDITING phrase. This independently defeats the fork even on the assumption that SR24 reaches the IS form: `9G9G9` declares ONE EDITING phrase, so it is one symbol under SR24 no matter how many times G appears. The fork fails on two independent grounds, not one.

4. THE PRECEDENCE NOTE — I verified the packet's factual premise and then found the reading self-defeating. The packet flagged §13.18.40.6's borrow of non-floating 'cs' precedence for 'es' as a residual counter-signal at MEDIUM-HIGH uncertainty. I checked Table 10 cell by cell rather than trusting the packet. Its premise is CORRECT: both non-floating cs rows have blanks in both cs columns, so cs cannot precede cs, and a mechanical borrow would bar es-after-es. But two things the packet missed dispose of it. (a) The note says to borrow "the column and row" — singular — while §13.18.40.6's own third paragraph states non-floating cs "appears in two columns and two rows" encoding leftmost-vs-rightmost position. The instruction cannot be executed as written; you cannot derive a prohibition from an instruction that does not say which cells to read. (b) Far more forcefully: in both non-floating cs rows the 'A X' column is blank, and in the 'A X' row both cs columns are blank — cs may neither precede nor follow A/X. Applied mechanically to the IS form, the borrow would make it impossible for any picture to contain both 'X' and character-1, which is the exact conjunction GR7 REQUIRES to define an alphanumeric-edited item (and GR10 for national-edited). The borrow would repeal two General Rules. It must be read as governing the non-floating FOR use of 'es' — where SR25/SR26 impose exactly the cs-like leftmost/rightmost discipline it describes. I would drop the packet's uncertainty on this point from MEDIUM-HIGH to LOW.

5. WHAT I CHECKED AND DID NOT FIND. I looked for a maximum-occurrence rule for character-1 anywhere in §13.18.40.3 (SR8–SR26): there is none; SR10 is a floor, SR11 is cross-phrase distinctness, SR23/SR24 are scoped to the built-ins and the FOR form. I checked whether SR26's two-way split ("For fixed editing sign control ... For extended editing sign control") might sweep the IS form into its first branch via SR12's label: it does not help the fork, since that branch speaks only of the currency symbol being preceded by '+' or '-' and imposes no occurrence cap. Annex F has no bearing. E.2 item 25 reserves EDITING at 2023, so there is no prior-edition behavior to reconcile.

6. ONE SOFT SPOT THE PACKET DID NOT FLAG — and it flagged the wrong one. GR14's IS-form sizing sentence reads "the size of literal-1 is counted in the size of the item", with no per-occurrence qualifier — unlike the floating clause, which spells out "plus one character for each repetition of character-1". A literalist could read `PIC 9G9G9 EDITING "G" IS "<>"` as size 5 (literal counted once) rather than 7. This is resolved, not forked: editing rule 3 states that simple insertion "results in the insertion character occupying the same character position in the edited item as the associated symbol occupies in character-string-1" — each occupying occurrence contributes its own positions, exactly as each 'B' in `XBXBX` contributes one. So size is 7. But this is the place a real implementation divergence would actually surface, and it deserves the flag the packet spent on the precedence note.
second.annexEvidence: Annex D.24 (lines 48133–48179): four examples, ALL using the FOR form — no `IS literal-1` example exists anywhere in D.24. I confirm the packet's honesty here. I add a qualification it omitted: D.24 introduces the repeated `LLLL` case with "If you do not want spaces following the leading symbol, you would use FLOATING symbols", and the 13-character sizing analysis ("6 for the first 'L', 3 for the next three") is GR14's FLOATING-insertion rule, not simple insertion. So D.24 proves repetition is legal in the floating mode of the FOR form — a third editing mode, distinct from the simple-insertion IS form at issue. It is weaker support for the IS form than the packet implied, and its counting point is better made normatively by SR25 (per-EDITING-phrase). Annex E.3.3 item 19 (line 50275) is the useful annex evidence: "a literal of any size for simple insertion and sign-sensitive fixed insertion" — two capabilities for the two inner options, IS = simple insertion. Annex F: no bearing. E.2 item 25 reserves EDITING at 2023, so the phrase is new in the 2023 edition and there is no cross-edition variance to reconcile; docs/VERSION_CHANGE_REFERENCE.md's 2014→2023-addition row is correct.
second.answer:
SPEC-RESOLVED, against the prohibition. `PIC 9G9G9 EDITING "G" IS "<>"` is LEGAL. I concur with the adjudication's outcome and with its recommendation not to spend an owner decision — but its stated grounds need correction before they are recorded.

WHAT INDEPENDENTLY CONVINCED ME (two mutually independent kills, either sufficient):

(1) SR24 SENTENCE 1 DOES NOT REACH THE IS FORM — but not for the reason given. The packet claims editing rule 3 alone resolves it. It does not: character-1 appears in BOTH rule 3's simple-insertion list AND rule 5's fixed-insertion list, and the packet omitted rule 5's first sentence, which is the fork's best text. The resolving move is the PARTITION — rule 5's "When character-1 is used, AND IS NOT A SIMPLE INSERTION CHARACTER, it represents literal-2, or literal-3" confines character-1's fixed-insertion role to the FOR form. Reinforcing this decisively, GR14's 'es' entry uses SR24's own phrase for a different referent: "For fixed editing sign control symbols, each character used in the symbol is counted in the size of the item" — "each character used in the symbol" can only mean '+','-','CR','DB' (CR/DB being two-character symbols), and cannot mean literal-1, already sized by the previous sentence. The General Rules thus use "fixed editing sign control symbols" to mean the built-ins. SR12 sentence 1 applies that label to something no operative rule so treats. This is a term-of-art collision, not a rule SR24 must be reconciled with — which is a better position than the packet's "drafting defect", since implementors should not have to declare the standard wrong.

(2) EVEN IF SR24 DID REACH IT, IT WOULD NOT BITE. SR25 — which the packet never cites — glosses SR24's count normatively: "When extended editing sign control symbols are used and two are specified, the first occurrence of the EDITING PHRASE shall be for the leftmost symbol ... and the second occurrence shall be for the rightmost." SR24 counts EDITING PHRASES. `9G9G9` declares one phrase, hence one symbol, however many times G appears. This is stronger and more direct than the packet's Annex D.24 inference and does not depend on resolving (1) at all.

CORROBORATING: SR10 is a floor with no cap; SR11 scopes distinctness across phrases, not occurrences; SR12's own non-FOR branch offers "at least two occurrences of ... character-1" as a validity criterion (permissive limb, but a rule cannot forbid what its own sub-rule tests for); GR7/GR10 with Table 7 make a categorically-sign-control character-1 impossible in the two categories those rules define; Annex E.3.3 item 19 states the IS/FOR = simple/fixed-sign intent.

THE PRECEDENCE CAVEAT SHOULD BE DOWNGRADED, NOT PRESERVED AT MEDIUM-HIGH. I verified the packet's Table 10 premise cell by cell and it is correct — non-floating cs has no self-intersection. But the reading is self-defeating on two grounds the packet missed. First, §13.18.40.6 instructs a borrow from "the column and row" (singular) of non-floating cs, while its own third paragraph states that symbol "appears in two columns and two rows"; the instruction cannot be mechanically executed, and a prohibition cannot rest on it. Second and conclusively: in both non-floating cs rows the 'A X' column is blank, and in the 'A X' row both cs columns are blank — cs may neither precede nor follow A/X. A mechanical borrow would make it impossible for any picture to contain both 'X' and character-1, the exact conjunction GR7 REQUIRES to define an alphanumeric-edited item. The borrow would repeal GR7 and GR10. It plainly governs the non-floating FOR use of 'es', where SR25/SR26 impose precisely that leftmost/rightmost discipline. Record this as closed, not as a live residual.

THE REAL RESIDUAL IS SIZING, WHICH THE PACKET DID NOT FLAG. GR14's IS-form clause reads "the size of literal-1 is counted in the size of the item" with no per-occurrence qualifier — unlike the floating clause, which spells out "plus one character for each repetition of character-1". A literalist could compute size 5 for `PIC 9G9G9 EDITING "G" IS "<>"` instead of 7. Editing rule 3 resolves it ("the insertion character occupying the same character position ... as the associated symbol occupies in character-string-1" — per occurrence, exactly as each 'B' in `XBXBX`), so this is not a fork. But it is where an implementation divergence would actually appear, and it is the flag worth carrying forward in place of the precedence note.

DOC CORRECTION: the packet is right that the C4 design must not frame this as an "exemption from SR24" — that concedes the wrong premise. But its proposed replacement citation (rule 3 as primary) is also wrong, because rule 5 sentence 1 puts character-1 in the fixed-insertion list too. Cite the PARTITION: §13.18.40.5 rule 3 together with rule 5's "and is not a simple insertion character" qualifier, plus GR14's 'es' entry showing "fixed editing sign control symbols" denotes the built-ins, plus SR25 for the per-phrase counting idiom.
second.implementationConsequence:
PictureAnalyzer / EDITING validation. The packet's items 1–8 are substantively correct; I amend the citations and add two items.

1. DO NOT enforce SR24 sentence 1 against an IS-form (literal-1) character-1. Its subject is '+','-','CR','DB' plus the one-currency-symbol cap (SR23; GR14 'es' sentence 3). SR24 sentence 2 applies only to the FOR form and counts EDITING PHRASES, not character occurrences — authority is SR25 ("the first occurrence of the EDITING phrase ... the second occurrence"), NOT the Annex D.24 inference the packet used. `LLLL9.99F` is two phrases (L, F), not five occurrences.

2. ALLOW N >= 1 occurrences of an IS-form character-1 wherever the precedence table admits a simple insertion symbol. Treat IS-form 'es' as a member of the simple-insertion class alongside 'B','0','/',',' for precedence and category determination. Enforce only SR10 (>= 1) and SR11 (distinct character-1 across phrases).

3. SIZING — per occurrence: each contributes len(literal-1) positions. `PIC 9G9G9 EDITING "G" IS "<>"` = 3 + 2*2 = 7. NOTE FOR THE IMPLEMENTOR (not in the packet): GR14's IS clause says only "the size of literal-1 is counted in the size of the item" with no per-occurrence qualifier, so this is an inference from editing rule 3's positional rule and the 'B' analogue in `XBXBX`, not a literal reading. Add a code comment saying so. Do NOT copy the currency symbol's first-occurrence-then-one-each rule, and do NOT copy the floating rule (GR14 last sentence) — that one governs the FOR form's floating use, which is what Annex D.24's `LLLL` demonstrates.

4. EDITING SEMANTICS (rule 3): each occurrence inserts literal-1 verbatim at its position, unconditionally, independent of sign. No Table 8 lookup, no sign branch. `MOVE 123` yields `1<>2<>3`.

5. CATEGORY: GR7/GR10 — an IS-form character-1 counts as a simple-insertion instance, so `PIC XGXGX EDITING "G" IS "<>"` is a valid alphanumeric-edited item (the analogue of `XBXBX`). GR13a — character-1 satisfies the "at least one symbol '9' and at least one instance of character-1" limb.

6. VALIDATE (GR15 'es'): non-FOR form, each position group corresponding to an occurrence is checked to contain literal-1 — per occurrence, sign-independent. The spec's plural "the character position (s)" supports this directly.

7. PRECEDENCE (§13.18.40.6 line 21008) — NEW, and the packet left this as an open worry rather than an instruction. Apply the non-floating-'cs' precedence borrow ONLY to the FOR/extended (non-floating sign-control) use of 'es'. Do NOT apply it to the IS form: mechanically applied there it forbids character-1 from either preceding or following 'A'/'X' (verified in Table 10: both non-floating cs rows blank in the 'A X' column; the 'A X' row blank in both cs columns), which would make GR7 and GR10 unsatisfiable. KEEP ENFORCING UNCHANGED: SR8 (character-1 domain), SR9 (literal <= 50; national iff USAGE NATIONAL or 'N'), SR12a (literal-2/literal-3 equal width), SR12b (FOR ⇒ mask ⊆ {character-1,'9','.',cs,'P','V','Z'}), SR12c (unspecified sign phrase defaults to spaces of the specified literal's width), SR12 last-a (no extended sign control on a floating-point edited item), SR25/SR26 (two-extended ordering, currency adjacency).

9. TESTS (feedback_conformance_tests_per_feature, same commit): positive golden `PIC 9G9G9 EDITING "G" IS "<>"` → size 7, `MOVE 123` → `1<>2<>3`; positive golden for the alphanumeric-edited analogue `PIC XGXGX` (this one specifically pins item 7 — it is the case the precedence borrow would wrongly reject); a per-occurrence VALIDATE golden; and negative goldens asserting SR24 STILL fires for the genuine cases (two built-in sign symbols; three EDITING phrases with extended sign control) so the narrowed scope is pinned in both directions.

10. DOC UPDATE (process rule 4, same change set): amend the C4 design note. Do NOT record "rule 3 resolves it" — rule 5 sentence 1 also lists character-1 as a fixed-insertion symbol, and a reviewer who finds that sentence will reopen the question. Record the PARTITION (rule 3 + rule 5's "and is not a simple insertion character"), GR14 'es' sentence 3 as proof that "fixed editing sign control symbols" denotes the built-ins in the operative rules, and SR25 as the independent per-phrase counting kill. State that SR24 never applied. Record the precedence-borrow analysis as CLOSED with the GR7-unsatisfiability reason, and record the GR14 sizing thinness as the known soft spot in its place. Also correct docs/rearchitecture/PHASE-13-remaining-waves-scout.md line 71 ("char-1 appearing exactly once (fixed, per SR24)") — true only for the FOR/non-floating case; docs/rearchitecture/PHASE-13-wave-c-scout.md line 285 already has the correct two-mode split.

adjudications.title: C4: may one EDITING phrase carry BOTH NEGATIVE and POSITIVE? and may the IS form float?

first.fork: C4-fork3-both-NEG-and-POS-and-floating — (a) may one EDITING FOR phrase carry BOTH NEGATIVE IS literal-2 and POSITIVE IS literal-3? (b) may the `EDITING character-1 IS literal-1` (fixed editing sign control) form FLOAT?

governingText.quote: a) Literal-2 and literal-3 shall occupy the same number of character positions.
governingText.bearing: (a) DECISIVE. A cross-literal size-agreement constraint is meaningless unless literal-2 and literal-3 can both be present for the SAME character-1 — the item's size (see the 'es' size GR) is only ambiguous when one character position must hold either literal. Two separate EDITING phrases (SR11: distinct character-1) each have their own positions and would need no such agreement.

governingText.quote: If only POSITIVE is specified, the default character for the unspecified phrase is the space character repeated for the number of characters in literal-2. If only NEGATIVE is specified, the default character for the unspecified phrase is the space character repeated the number of characters in literal-3.
governingText.bearing: (a) DECISIVE. 'If ONLY POSITIVE is specified' / 'the unspecified phrase' presuppose a case in which the phrase is NOT only-one — i.e. both. Under an exclusive-choice reading exactly one is always unspecified and the word 'only' plus the two-branch structure would be dead text. (The literal-2/literal-3 cross-reference in this rule is an evident editorial slip — the defaulted length is that of the literal that WAS specified; Table 8/9's 'literal-2 or literal-3 or spaces' gloss confirms.)

governingText.quote: If more than one EDITING phrase is specified in one PICTURE clause, no two instances of character-1 shall be the same character.
governingText.bearing: (a) Shows the mechanism for multiple phrases is repetition of the whole EDITING phrase (the '...' after the outer bracket in the Format-1 diagram), each with a DIFFERENT character-1 — so the ellipsis does not supply the NEGATIVE+POSITIVE combination, and SR12 a)/c) cannot be explained away as inter-phrase rules.

governingText.quote: Braces, { }, enclosing a portion of a general format indicate that the syntax element contained within the braces or one of the alternatives contained within the braces shall be explicitly specified or is implicitly selected. … Choice indicators are a pair of bars, |, that enclose a portion of a general format. When enclosed by braces, one or more of the alternatives contained within the choice indicators shall be specified, but any single alternative shall be specified only once. … The alternatives may be specified in any order.
governingText.bearing: (a) The notation clause supplies exactly the construct SR12 a)/c) presume — braces around choice indicators = one OR MORE, each at most once, any order. The apparent conflict is an artifact of the prose transcription of the figure at line 20248, which does not record the bars.

governingText.section: 13.18.40.5 Editing rules, rule 6 (Floating insertion editing), spec line ~20812
governingText.quote: The currency symbol, the extended editing sign control symbols, if specified, and the fixed editing sign control symbols '+' and '-' are used as the floating insertion symbols.
governingText.bearing: (b) DECISIVE. The list of floating insertion symbols is closed. It admits the EXTENDED editing sign control symbol (SR12: character-1 with the FOR phrase) but, among fixed editing sign control symbols, names only '+' and '-'. Character-1 with IS literal-1 — which SR12 calls a fixed editing sign control symbol — is NOT in the list, so it cannot float. Conversely this same sentence positively AUTHORIZES the FOR-form 'es' to float.

governingText.section: 13.18.40.5 Editing rules, rule 3 (Simple insertion editing), spec line ~20762
governingText.quote: Character-1 and the symbols 'B', '0', '/', ',' and, if literal=1 [literal-1] is specified, character-1 are used as the simple insertion editing symbols.
governingText.bearing: (b) Classifies the IS form (literal-1) as SIMPLE insertion. (a) YES — one EDITING FOR phrase may carry BOTH `NEGATIVE IS literal-2` and `POSITIVE IS literal-3`. The resolving sentences are SR12 a) ("Literal-2 and literal-3 shall occupy the same number of character positions") and SR12 c) ("If only POSITIVE is specified … the unspecified phrase …"), each of which is inoperative text under an exclusive-choice reading, and neither of which can be reinterpreted as an inter-phrase rule because SR11 forces distinct character-1 per phrase. Implement: accept NEGATIVE and/or POSITIVE, either order, each at most once per phrase; diagnose a repeated NEGATIVE or repeated POSITIVE within one phrase; diagnose length(literal-2) != length(literal-3) when both are present (SR12 a)); when only one is present, synthesize the other as spaces of the specified literal's length (SR12 c), confirmed by D.24's 'bbbbbb123.45').

(b) NO for the IS form; YES for the FOR form. `EDITING character-1 IS literal-1` may NOT float. Decisive sentence: editing rule 6 — "The currency symbol, the extended editing sign control symbols, if specified, and the fixed editing sign control symbols '+' and '-' are used as the floating insertion symbols" — a closed list that includes the extended (FOR) symbol but, of the fixed editing sign control symbols, only '+' and '-'. Correspondingly the FOR-form es DOES float, per that same rule 6, Table 9, and Annex D.24's `PIC IS LLLL9.99F`.

Correction to the fork's stated premise: the Table 10 precedence note at line 21010 is NOT decisive for (b) and must not be cited as the prohibition. It assigns 'es' a precedence class for ordering purposes only; Table 10 never governs symbol repetition, and repetition is the sole trigger for floating. Read as a floating ban it would contradict rule 6, Table 9's caption, the size GR and D.24. Also correct the C4 design's reading of the SR12 non-FOR branch: its "at least two occurrences of one of the symbols from the set character-1, 'X', '+', '-', and the currency symbol" is a minimum-content syntax rule about what character-string-1 shall CONTAIN; it does not confer floating semantics on the IS form, and cannot override the General rules (per line 2774, the Editing rules are General rules) that assign the editing type.

So the packet's conclusion survives its strongest available attack.

Where the packet is WRONG is its dismissal of the Table 10 note. It asserts 'Table 10 governs which symbol may PRECEDE which; it never governs repetition.' That is false. The Table 10 preamble reads 'the symbol(s) at the top of the column may precede (but not necessarily immediately) in character-string-1 the symbol(s) at the left of the row' — a symbol preceding ITSELF is exactly the self-intersection cell, and the floating cs/cs, Z*/Z*, and +−/+− self-cells are precisely what make '$$$$', 'ZZZZ' and '++++' legal, while the non-floating cs row carries no x in the non-floating cs column. Applied literally, therefore, the note ('es … has the same precedence as the cs symbol in the column and row of non-floating insertion symbols') WOULD make 'LLLL' illegal. And §13.18.40.6's opening ('Where an x appears … additional syntax rules or general rules may apply further restrictions') is one-directional, so other rules cannot simply add the missing x. This is a real internal inconsistency in the standard, not a mis-scoped rule.

It does not change the answer. One precedence note versus editing rule 6 naming es as a floating insertion symbol, Table 9's caption calling es a floating editing sign control symbol, Table 9's es rows, the size GR's floating clause for literal-2/literal-3, and a worked Annex D.24 example whose arithmetic reproduces that GR — the note loses on overwhelming weight, and the only coherent harmonization is that the note supplies es's precedence relative to OTHER symbols (es has no row/column of its own) and does not reach es-vs-es, which rule 6 governs directly. But the reason must be recorded honestly as 'the note is defective / read narrowly', not as 'Table 10 does not govern repetition'. Recording the wrong reason would mislead whoever next touches the precedence checker.
second.answer:
SPEC-RESOLVED, both parts. I AGREE with the adjudication's conclusions and with essentially all of its implementation consequences. No owner decision is warranted. Three corrections to the record.

(a) YES — one EDITING FOR phrase may carry BOTH `NEGATIVE IS literal-2` and `POSITIVE IS literal-3`. What independently convinced me is not the packet's inference but the primary source: I rendered PDF page 471 (printed page 441) and the Format 1 diagram plainly shows a pair of VERTICAL BARS enclosing the stacked NEGATIVE/POSITIVE alternatives inside the FOR braces. Per §5.2.6.4, braces enclosing choice indicators mean 'one or more of the alternatives … shall be specified, but any single alternative shall be specified only once … in any order.' The repo's OCR at line 20248 simply lost the bars. The packet's stated residual risk ('if the printed figure genuinely uses bare braces the standard is internally inconsistent') is retired: the bars are there, and the standard is consistent. SR12 a) and c) drop from load-bearing to corroborating. The outer brace (`IS literal-1` vs `FOR`) has no bars, so those two remain mutually exclusive.

CORRECTION 1: SR12 c)'s literal-2/literal-3 cross-reference is not necessarily an editorial slip. It names the unspecified phrase's OWN literal identifier, and SR12 a) forces the two lengths equal, so the count is determinate from the literal that was supplied. Same implementation either way; D.24's 'bbbbbb123.45' (6 = len("DEBIT ")) fixes it.

(b) NO for the IS form; YES for the FOR form. `EDITING character-1 IS literal-1` may NOT float. Decisive: editing rule 6's closed floating-symbol list includes the extended (FOR) es but, among fixed editing sign control symbols, only '+' and '-'. That the enumeration is a selection rather than an illustration is confirmed by CR and DB — also fixed editing sign control symbols per Table 8 — being equally absent. Independently confirmed by editing rule 3 (literal-1 ⇒ simple insertion), by the line-20595 size GR (a floating computation exists only for literal-2/literal-3), and by Table 9 having no row for the IS form. The FOR-form es DOES float, per rule 6, Table 9's caption and rows, and Annex D.24's `PIC IS LLLL9.99F` ⇒ 'b(123.45)'. I additionally stress-tested this against SR12's non-FOR minimum-content bullet ('at least two occurrences of … character-1, x, +, -, and the currency symbol'), the best available counter-argument; it fails because 'x' is in the same set and two X's float nothing — it is a syntax minimum, and per 5.3.3 the Editing rules are General rules that assign the editing type.

CORRECTION 2 (the substantive refutation): the packet's reason for dismissing the Table 10 note is wrong and must not be recorded. It claims 'Table 10 never governs repetition.' Table 10's preamble governs any column symbol preceding any row symbol, itself included, and the floating cs/cs, Z*/Z*, +−/+− self-intersections are exactly what license '$$$$', 'ZZZZ', '++++'; the non-floating cs row has no x in the non-floating cs column. So the note, read literally, WOULD outlaw 'LLLL'. Combined with §13.18.40.6's one-directional opening sentence ('additional syntax rules or general rules may apply further restrictions'), this is a genuine defect in the standard. The outcome is unchanged — rule 6, Table 9, the size GR and D.24 overwhelm one precedence note — but the note must be documented as a narrow/defective provision that supplies es's precedence relative to OTHER symbols only, with es-vs-es governed directly by rule 6.

CORRECTION 3: the packet's 'the OCR transcription is demonstrably lossy' evidence is largely wrong. I checked printed pages 442, 473 and 483: 'at least on one', the duplicated 'a)' in SR12, 'literal=1', and the redundant leading 'Character-1' in editing rule 3 are all in the PRINTED standard. The OCR is faithful for prose; only the figure's choice bars were dropped. Standing lesson for this repo: trust specs/ISO_COBOL.md for rule text, render the PDF page image whenever a general-format DIAGRAM is load-bearing.

second.implementationConsequence:
I endorse the packet's implementation consequences with the amendments below.

Grammar/parser. Model the FOR phrase as choice-indicator semantics, not an exclusive alternative: `FOR ( NEGATIVE IS lit2 )? ( POSITIVE IS lit3 )?` with at least one present, either order, each at most once. Keep `IS literal-1` and `FOR ...` mutually exclusive (the outer brace in the printed figure has no bars). Keep the whole `EDITING character-1 [ ... ]` group repeatable per the trailing ellipsis (§5.2.7 scopes it to the bracketed EDITING group).

Binder/validation diagnostics. (1) SR12 a): if both NEGATIVE and POSITIVE are present, require length(literal-2) == length(literal-3). (2) Reject a duplicated NEGATIVE or duplicated POSITIVE within one phrase (§5.2.6.4 'only once'). (3) SR12 c): when only one polarity is given, synthesize the other as a spaces literal of the SAME LENGTH AS THE SPECIFIED LITERAL — do not follow the printed cross-reference literally; D.24's 'bbbbbb123.45' fixes this. (4) SR11: distinct character-1 across phrases. (5) SR10: character-1 shall appear at least once in character-string-1. (6) SR12 b): with FOR, character-string-1 shall contain character-1 and only '9', '.', cs, 'P', 'V', 'Z'. (7) SR12 (second 'a)'): with FOR, no editing sign control symbols in character-string-1, and no extended es on a floating-point edited item. (8) SR24/25: at most two es symbols (two EDITING phrases); when two, the first phrase is for the leftmost symbol and the second for the rightmost. (9) SR8/SR9: character-1 restrictions and the national/alphanumeric literal + 50-char cap.

PICTURE symbol classification (load-bearing). character-1 with `IS literal-1` ⇒ SIMPLE-INSERTION class ONLY. Never enter the floating-string builder for it, even with 2+ occurrences; each occurrence emits literal-1 at its own position and contributes length(literal-1) to the item size. character-1 with `FOR` ⇒ FIXED-INSERTION class; when it occurs in a string of 2+ identical occurrences (rule 6, absorbing embedded and immediately-right simple-insertion symbols) ⇒ FLOATING class.

Size computation for a floating es run of N identical character-1's (line 20595, arithmetic verified against D.24): length(literal) + (N - 1). D.24's 'LLLL' with a 6-char literal ⇒ 6 + 3 = 9, plus 4 numeric/insertion positions = 13. For the non-floating FOR case, each occurrence contributes the full literal length. Retain the run boundaries so the emitter reserves the first slot for the literal and treats the remaining N-1 as data/space positions.

Runtime edit results. Fixed es (Table 8): NEGATIVE phrase ⇒ literal-2 on negative, literal-2-or-spaces on positive/zero; POSITIVE phrase ⇒ literal-3 on positive/zero, literal-3-or-spaces on negative; 'or spaces' means exactly as many spaces as the literal has characters (Table 8's own gloss). Floating es (Table 9): same polarity mapping, single literal placed immediately left of the first significant position per rule 6 a)/b), preceding positions spaces; rule 6 b) all-numeric-positions-floating ⇒ all spaces when the value is zero.

Precedence checker — AMENDED, and this is where I diverge from the packet's rationale. Give 'es' the NON-FLOATING 'cs' row/column entries for ordering against OTHER symbols (the Table 10 note), but hard-code an exception permitting es to precede itself, and add a source comment recording WHY: the Table 10 note, applied literally, would forbid 'LLLL' because the non-floating cs row carries no x in the non-floating cs column, yet editing rule 6 (a General rule per 5.3.3), Table 9, the line-20595 size GR and Annex D.24 all require floating es. Document this as a defect in the standard resolved in favour of rule 6 — do NOT record the packet's reason ('Table 10 does not govern repetition'), which is false: Table 10's self-intersection cells are exactly what license '$$$$', 'ZZZZ' and '++++'.

De-editing / VALIDATE format validation (line 20687): without FOR, check character-1's positions contain literal-1; with FOR, check the negative-result positions against literal-2 and the positive-result positions against literal-3, per the Table 8/Table 9 mapping actually in force for that item.

Conformance tests to ship in the same change set: both-polarities-in-one-phrase (accepted; unequal lengths diagnosed); duplicated NEGATIVE diagnosed; POSITIVE-before-NEGATIVE accepted; the four D.24 cases reproduced byte-for-byte ('(b123.45)', 'b(123.45)', 'DEBIT 123.45', 'bbbbbb123.45'); the D.24 size case asserting 13; a 2+-occurrence IS form asserting N independent simple insertions and size N*len(literal-1), NOT a floating run.
