adjudications.title: C5: does the FINALLY phrase of an exception-checking PERFORM run on the FATAL path?

first.fork: C5-fork1-FINALLY-on-fatal-path — does the FINALLY phrase of an exception-checking (Format 3) PERFORM execute on the fatal/unhandled path, i.e. must FINALLY be emitted as a C# `finally` block or as plain sequential code at the end of the PERFORM?

governingText.quote: If the FINALLY phrase is specified, the end of the PERFORM statement begins at imperative-statement-5. There shall be no statements that include a transfer of control out of the PERFORM statement within imperative-statement-5. Any EXIT PERFORM statement within imperative-statement-5 transfers control to an implicit CONTINUE statement following the END-PERFORM. If the FINALLY phrase is not specified, the end of the PERFORM statement is indicated by END-PERFORM.
governingText.bearing: THE load-bearing rule. FINALLY is not a separate construct with its own reachability rule — it IS 'the end of the PERFORM statement'. Therefore FINALLY executes exactly when, and only when, some other rule says control 'proceeds/passes to the end of the PERFORM statement'. Every other question reduces to: does control reach the end of the PERFORM?

governingText.quote: The end of the PERFORM statement includes the statements in a FINALLY phrase, if it is specified.
governingText.bearing: Confirms the GR16 identity explicitly, so 'control passes to the end of the PERFORM statement' in GR18/GR20 is not a way of saying 'past END-PERFORM'.

governingText.quote: If execution of the last statement in imperative-statement-1 completes successfully, execution proceeds to the end of the PERFORM statement. If an exception-condition was raised during the processing of imperative-statement-1 that caused a transfer to the imperative-statement in a WHEN phrase, and the processing in General rules 17, 18, and 19 is completed, return depends on whether the exception condition was fatal or nonfatal. If the exception condition was nonfatal, execution continues with an implicit CONTINUE statement immediately following the statement in imperative-statement-1 in which the exception condition occurred. If that statement was the last statement in imperative-statement-1, execution continues at the end of the PERFORM statement. If the exception condition was fatal, execution continues as specified in 14.6.13.1.3, Fatal exception conditions.
governingText.bearing: Settles cases (i) and (ii). Normal completion -> end of PERFORM -> FINALLY runs. Nonfatal handled by WHEN -> resume inside imperative-statement-1 -> eventually falls into the end of PERFORM -> FINALLY runs. Fatal handled by WHEN -> control is handed to 14.6.13.1.3, NOT to the end of the PERFORM. GR20 never routes the fatal case to the end of the PERFORM.

governingText.quote: If the executed statement is within imperative-statement-1 of a PERFORM statement that contains a WHEN phrase that specifies the exception-name associated with the exception condition or an exception-name of a higher level in the same hierarchy, the imperative statement in the WHEN phrase is executed. If WHEN COMMON is specified, the imperative-statement within the COMMON phrase is executed. Execution of the last imperative statement is terminated abnormally as specified in 14.6.12, Abnormal run unit termination.
governingText.bearing: Case (ii)-fatal. After the WHEN (and WHEN COMMON) handler, the run unit terminates abnormally at the end of that handler. It does NOT say the PERFORM statement completes, and control therefore never reaches GR16's imperative-statement-5. FINALLY does not run.

governingText.quote: 5) If checking for the exception condition is enabled and there is an applicable USE statement ... the associated declarative is executed. If execution of the declarative completes normally the execution of the run unit is terminated abnormally ... 6) ... there is an applicable PROPAGATE ON directive, the exception condition is propagated as if a GOBACK statement with the RAISING LAST EXCEPTION phrase were executed. 7) If checking for the exception condition is enabled, execution of the run unit is terminated abnormally as specified in 14.6.12, Abnormal run unit termination.
governingText.bearing: Case (iii)-fatal (unmatched by any WHEN, no WHEN OTHER). Item 4 does not apply, so the ordered list falls through to 5/6/7: declarative-then-abend, propagate out of the runtime element, or abend. All three leave the PERFORM without reaching its end. FINALLY does not run.

governingText.quote: If a conditional phrase without the NOT phrase is specified in the interrupted statement and the rules for that statement indicate that the fatal exception condition is to be processed by the conditional phrase, the procedures for nonfatal exceptions as specified in 14.6.13.1.4, Nonfatal exception conditions, apply.
governingText.bearing: The verifier's point. Because the list is ORDERED, a fatal condition on a statement carrying ON SIZE ERROR / AT END / INVALID KEY etc. is demoted to nonfatal processing BEFORE item 4 is ever consulted. That path then follows 14.6.13.1.4 item 4 ('Execution of the statement continues as specified in the rules for that statement') back into imperative-statement-1, and FINALLY DOES run. So 'the exception is fatal' is not by itself sufficient to suppress FINALLY.

governingText.quote: If the exception condition is a fatal EC-I-O exception condition, then the rules for 9.1.13, I-O status apply, then if the implementor has not specified otherwise, the following rules apply for all fatal exception conditions.
governingText.bearing: The second ordering carve-out: fatal EC-I-O goes through I-O status first, and the implementor may specify otherwise (cf. Annex D: 'Some latitude is given to implementors to specify alternative treatment of fatal exceptions, in particular for input-output exceptions'). Implementor latitude, not a spec ambiguity — but it means the fatal-EC-I-O row is a documented CONFORMANCE.md choice, not an unconditional abend.

governingText.quote: 2) If the executed statement is within imperative-statement-1 of a PERFORM statement that contains a WHEN phrase ... the imperative statement in the WHEN phrase is executed. Execution of the imperative statement in the WHEN phrase completes as specified in the rules for the PERFORM statement. ... 3) If there is an applicable USE statement ... 4) Execution of the statement continues as specified in the rules for that statement.
governingText.bearing: Case (iii)-nonfatal. An unmatched NONFATAL exception falls to item 3/4 and execution continues inside imperative-statement-1, so control still falls into the end of the PERFORM and FINALLY runs. The fatal/nonfatal split, not the matched/unmatched split, is what decides FINALLY.

governingText.quote: If an EXIT PERFORM statement is specified in an exception-checking PERFORM statement, control passes to an implicit CONTINUE statement immediately preceding the END-PERFORM phrase specified for that PERFORM statement or, if the FINALLY phrase is specified, immediately preceding the FINALLY phrase.
governingText.bearing: Case (iv), the sanctioned intra-PERFORM branch. EXIT PERFORM from imperative-statement-1 OR from any WHEN / WHEN OTHER / WHEN COMMON handler jumps to just BEFORE imperative-statement-5, so FINALLY runs and the remaining handler phrases (notably WHEN COMMON) are SKIPPED. Note the deliberate asymmetry with GR16: EXIT PERFORM inside FINALLY itself lands AFTER END-PERFORM.

governingText.quote: Any exception conditions raised during the execution of imperative-statement-2, imperative-statement-3, imperative-statement-4, or imperative-statement-5 will not cause transfer of control to any of these imperative-statements. The results are as if these statements were specified in a format 2 PERFORM statement.
governingText.bearing: A fatal exception raised inside a WHEN handler or inside FINALLY itself is processed by ordinary 14.6.13.1.3 machinery (declarative / PROPAGATE / abend) with no FINALLY re-entry — reinforcing that FINALLY has no protected-region semantics.

governingText.quote: If control is transferred outside of the PERFORM during WHEN processing, exceptions can occur. These will be processed by whatever mechanism is normally used for this processing (such as a USE or TURN directive that can cause transfer of control to some place in the program that would never hit the exit of this PERFORM or a CALL to a program that raises an exception). The user is advised to avoid transfers outside of the PERFORM for WHEN processing.
governingText.bearing: Explicitly contemplates control going 'some place in the program that would never hit the exit of this PERFORM' and merely ADVISES against it rather than defining a FINALLY-runs-anyway rule. Decisive against C#-finally semantics for GO TO / GOBACK out of imperative-statement-1 or a WHEN.

governingText.quote: The RESUME statement transfers control to a procedure-name or to the statement following the statement that caused a declarative or an imperative-statement in a WHEN phrase of an exception-checking PERFORM statement to be executed. ... The RESUME statement may be specified only in a declarative or in an imperative statement in a WHEN phrase of an exception-checking PERFORM statement. In the latter case, the NEXT STATEMENT phrase shall be specified. ... NOTE 1 The user is able to continue by using a RESUME statement, although this might not be advisable for most fatal conditions.
governingText.bearing: The escape hatch that makes a FATAL, WHEN-matched exception still reach FINALLY: RESUME AT NEXT STATEMENT in the handler transfers control back into imperative-statement-1 after the raising statement, pre-empting item 4's abnormal termination; execution then falls into the end of the PERFORM and FINALLY runs. A fifth emitter case, not covered by the four in the question.

governingText.section: Annex D.16.5 Inline exception processing (informative EXAMPLE) — first listing
governingText.quote:
WHEN COMMON
   >* come here if either WHEN phrase was entered
   Some statements
   >* exception fatal: run unit terminates
   >* exception nonfatal: control is passed
   >*   to **next statement**
FINALLY
   *> come here for no matching exceptions
   *> of if an EXIT PERFORM was in a WHEN
governingText.bearing: SETTLES IT. The committee's own worked example places 'exception fatal: run unit terminates' at the END OF WHEN COMMON, with FINALLY drawn below it and annotated as reached only for 'no matching exceptions' or an EXIT PERFORM in a WHEN. A conforming implementation with C#-finally semantics would print the FINALLY text on the fatal path; this example says the run unit terminates instead.

governingText.section: Annex D.16.5 — second listing ('You could avoid termination with something like this')
governingText.quote:
WHEN EC-SIZE
    >* here when the size error occurred
    Some statements
    RESUME AT NEXT STATEMENT >* go to next statement
 ... FINALLY
    *> come here for no matching exceptions
    >* or a nonfatal was processed
 ... If you specified EXIT PERFORM in a WHEN, execution would proceed at FINALLY.
governingText.bearing: Confirms the two additional FINALLY-reaching paths and the framing that RESUME is what 'avoids termination' — i.e. absent RESUME, termination (and no FINALLY) is the fatal-path behavior. The closing sentence independently confirms §14.9.14.4 GR4 for EXIT PERFORM inside a WHEN.

first.derivation:
1. GR16 + NOTE 8 collapse the question: FINALLY IS 'the end of the PERFORM statement'. So FINALLY executes iff control reaches the end of the PERFORM. There is no rule anywhere in §14.9.28 or §14.6.13 granting FINALLY protected-region / unwind-time semantics. Grepping FINALLY across the whole spec returns 12 hits and they are exhaustively: the syntax diagram, GR16, NOTE 8, GR21, §14.9.14.4 GR4, Annex D.16.5, and index/TOC lines. Nothing else.

2. Case (i) normal completion — GR20 sentence 1: 'If execution of the last statement in imperative-statement-1 completes successfully, execution proceeds to the end of the PERFORM statement.' => FINALLY RUNS.

3. Case (ii) exception caught by WHEN / WHEN OTHER / WHEN COMMON — GR17/18/19 run the handler(s), then GR20 splits on fatality:
   - NONFATAL: 'execution continues with an implicit CONTINUE statement immediately following the statement in imperative-statement-1 in which the exception condition occurred. If that statement was the last statement ..., execution continues at the end of the PERFORM statement.' => control re-enters imperative-statement-1 and ultimately falls into the end => FINALLY RUNS.
   - FATAL: 'execution continues as specified in 14.6.13.1.3'. Reading that subclause IN ORDER, as the verifier demanded: item 1 first demotes the case to nonfatal handling if the interrupted statement carries a non-NOT conditional phrase (ON SIZE ERROR etc.) that the statement's own rules say handles it — that path ends at 14.6.13.1.4 item 4 and DOES reach FINALLY. Item 2 hands MERGE/SORT off. Item 3 routes fatal EC-I-O through 9.1.13 with explicit implementor latitude. Only if none of 1-3 divert does item 4 apply, and item 4 ends: 'Execution of the last imperative statement is terminated abnormally as specified in 14.6.12.' Termination occurs at the end of the WHEN/COMMON handler; the PERFORM statement never completes; GR16's imperative-statement-5 is never reached => FINALLY DOES NOT RUN.

4. Case (iii) exception matched by NO WHEN phrase — note first that if WHEN OTHER is present this case is empty for enabled exceptions (GR18 routes them to imperative-statement-3), and per GR14 only exceptions enabled at the point of detection are processed at all, so a genuinely unmatched exception requires an explicit TURN directive.
   - NONFATAL unmatched: 14.6.13.1.4 items 3/4 — declarative if any, else 'Execution of the statement continues as specified in the rules for that statement' => stays in imperative-statement-1, falls into the end => FINALLY RUNS.
   - FATAL unmatched: 14.6.13.1.3 item 4 does not apply (no matching WHEN), so the ordered list continues to item 5 (declarative, then abend on normal completion), item 6 (PROPAGATE ON => propagate as GOBACK RAISING LAST EXCEPTION, leaving the runtime element entirely), item 7 (abend). None returns control to the end of the PERFORM => FINALLY DOES NOT RUN. (Item 8, checking not enabled, cannot arise here since a WHEN or TURN is what enabled it.)

5. Case (iv) transfer of control out of the PERFORM — two distinct sub-cases that the original claim conflates:
   - EXIT PERFORM (the sanctioned intra-statement branch): §14.9.14.4 GR4 sends it 'immediately preceding the FINALLY phrase', from imperative-statement-1 or from ANY handler phrase => FINALLY RUNS, and any not-yet-executed handler phrases (WHEN COMMON in particular) are SKIPPED. Annex D's closing sentence confirms. GR16 inverts this inside FINALLY itself: EXIT PERFORM there lands after END-PERFORM.
   - A true transfer out (GO TO out of range, GOBACK, EXIT PROGRAM, STOP RUN, or a propagated exception) from imperative-statement-1 or a handler: no rule makes FINALLY run, and NOTE 9 expressly contemplates control going 'some place in the program that would never hit the exit of this PERFORM' while only ADVISING users against it => FINALLY DOES NOT RUN. GR16 bans such transfers only WITHIN imperative-statement-5, not within imperative-statement-1.

6. Annex D.16.5 independently settles the contested case with an informative example: the fatal outcome is annotated at the bottom of WHEN COMMON as 'exception fatal: run unit terminates', while the FINALLY block below is annotated 'come here for no matching exceptions / or if an EXIT PERFORM was in a WHEN' — and the SECOND listing frames RESUME AT NEXT STATEMENT as how 'You could avoid termination', with FINALLY then annotated 'or a nonfatal was processed'. A C#-`finally` implementation would execute imperative-statement-5 on the fatal path and contradict both listings.

7. There is therefore no second defensible reading. The claim's CONCLUSION (plain sequential code, not a C# finally) is correct, but its stated DERIVATION (item 4 alone) is too narrow and would mis-handle the item-1 demotion, the RESUME escape hatch, and the EXIT PERFORM entry edge.
first.answer:
SPEC-RESOLVED — and it resolves IN FAVOUR of the C5 design's emitter shape, while invalidating the design's stated derivation.

The single sentence that resolves it is §14.9.28.4 GR16: 'If the FINALLY phrase is specified, the end of the PERFORM statement begins at imperative-statement-5' (with NOTE 8 confirming). FINALLY has no unwind semantics of its own; it runs iff control reaches the end of the PERFORM statement. The fatal path per §14.6.13.1.3 items 4 / 5-7 terminates the run unit (or propagates out) without the PERFORM completing, so FINALLY does not run. Annex D.16.5's worked example states this outright: 'exception fatal: run unit terminates' sits at the end of WHEN COMMON, and FINALLY is annotated 'come here for no matching exceptions of if an EXIT PERFORM was in a WHEN'.

The four-way (really six-way) answer the emitter shape depends on:
(i)   NORMAL completion of imperative-statement-1 -> FINALLY RUNS. §14.9.28.4 GR20 sentence 1.
(ii)  Exception CAUGHT by WHEN / WHEN OTHER / WHEN COMMON:
        - nonfatal -> FINALLY RUNS (via resumption at the implicit CONTINUE after the raising statement, then fall-through). GR20 sentences 3-4.
        - fatal     -> FINALLY DOES NOT RUN; abnormal run-unit termination at the end of the last handler. §14.6.13.1.3 item 4 + GR20 last sentence.

second.derivation:
I attacked the adjudication on all four axes the task specifies. On quotation fidelity it survives cleanly: I pulled every cited passage from specs/ISO_COBOL.md and every quote is verbatim, untruncated, and in context. The Annex D listings in particular are reproduced exactly, including the typo 'of if an EXIT PERFORM was in a WHEN'.

On missed rules, I found three the adjudication did not quote, one of which is a genuine problem.

(1) GR18 IS SELF-CONTRADICTORY AND THE ADJUDICATION NEVER QUOTED IT. This is the best available refutation of SPEC-RESOLVED, so I pressed it hard. GR18 sentence 2 says 'At the completion of the execution of imperative-statement-3, control is passed to the end of the PERFORM statement or, if WHEN COMMON is specified, to imperative-statement-4.' By GR16 + NOTE 8, 'the end of the PERFORM statement' IS imperative-statement-5. Read literally and standalone, GR18 says that after a WHEN OTHER handler with no WHEN COMMON present, FINALLY runs — unconditionally, fatal or not. That flatly contradicts GR20's fatal routing and would make the fork genuine for the WHEN-OTHER-without-COMMON sub-case.

I concluded it is an editorial defect rather than a fork, on four grounds. First, the two sentences are consecutive, near-identical, and mutually exclusive — the signature of a revision where the superseded sentence was not deleted. Second, the replacement sentence's cross-reference, 'General rule 14.9.29', is malformed on its face: 14.9.29 is a clause number (the RAISE statement, which I confirmed at line 29723), not a general rule number. The intended referent is unmistakably 14.9.28.4 GR20, because GR17 and GR19 — the exactly parallel rules for WHEN and WHEN COMMON — both read 'control is passed as indicated in General rule 20'. GR18 is the odd one out purely by a mis-substituted number. Third, harmonizing GR18 with its two siblings is the only reading under which the three handler-completion rules are consistent with each other. Fourth, Annex D.16.5's first listing includes a WHEN OTHER, and its fatal outcome is annotated 'run unit terminates', not FINALLY. So the tie IS broken, by GR17/GR19 parallelism plus Annex D. The correct implementation is GR18-as-GR20; but this is a spec defect worth recording, not an owner decision.

(2) GR14's implicit POP ALL is sited 'immediately preceding the END PERFORM phrase' — a fixed textual position, not an unwind hook. Nobody drafting a protected-region construct writes the state-restore that way. This is independent structural evidence for the conclusion that the adjudication did not use. It also has a consequence the adjudication missed: since POP ALL sits after imperative-statement-5, FINALLY executes with WHEN checking still enabled.

(3) Annex D.16.5's preamble sentence corroborates the item-1 demotion directly rather than by inference.

On over-reading, I checked whether GR16 is being over-read. It is not: 'the end of the PERFORM statement BEGINS AT imperative-statement-5' is a definitional identity, and NOTE 8 restates it. Every downstream rule that says 'control is passed to the end of the PERFORM statement' therefore mechanically means 'FINALLY runs', and every path that does not say that means it does not.

I also probed the one place Annex D could be read against the conclusion. FINALLY's annotation 'come here for no matching exceptions' could be read as 'an exception occurred but matched no WHEN' — which would flip case (iii)-fatal. It cannot mean that here: the listing contains a WHEN OTHER, so with checking enabled no exception can go unmatched (GR18 routes all of them to imperative-statement-3). Combined with the imperative-statement-1 annotation 'more statements / execution goes to FINALLY', 'no matching exceptions' can only mean 'no exception was raised'. Loose informative prose, not a contradiction of items 5/6/7.

Finally I verified the item-4 reading is not being strained. 'Execution of the last imperative statement is terminated abnormally as specified in 14.6.12' — 'the last imperative statement' is the last handler executed (WHEN, or WHEN COMMON if present). Termination happens at the END of that handler. The PERFORM statement never completes, so GR16's imperative-statement-5 is unreachable. There is a mild circularity — GR20 sends the fatal case to 14.6.13.1.3, whose item 4 says to execute the handler we have already executed — but the net effect (abend at the end of the handler) is identical under either resolution, and Annex D states that net effect outright.
second.answer:
SPEC-RESOLVED. I independently reach the same classification and the same answer as the adjudication under review, and I also endorse its correction of the original C5 claim's derivation.

What independently convinced me, beyond re-reading its cited text: (a) the GR14 POP-ALL siting — the spec places the exception-checking state restore at a fixed textual position 'immediately preceding the END PERFORM phrase' rather than at unwind, which is architecturally incompatible with a protected-region reading and which the adjudication never used; (b) the Annex D.16.5 preamble sentence, which states the ON-SIZE-ERROR-suppresses-WHEN behavior directly rather than leaving it to be inferred from the item-1 ordering; and (c) my own failed attempt to break the tie in the other direction — the strongest counter-text I could find (GR18 sentence 1) turns out to be a demonstrably defective sentence rather than a competing reading.

THE RESOLVING SENTENCE is §14.9.28.4 GR16: 'If the FINALLY phrase is specified, the end of the PERFORM statement begins at imperative-statement-5', with NOTE 8 confirming. FINALLY has no unwind semantics; it runs if and only if control reaches the end of the PERFORM statement. §14.6.13.1.3 items 4 and 5-7 terminate the run unit or propagate out without the PERFORM completing, so FINALLY does not run on the fatal path. Annex D.16.5 states this outright.

The per-case answer (I confirm all six of the adjudication's rows):
(i) normal completion of imperative-statement-1 -> FINALLY RUNS (GR20 sentence 1).
(ii) exception caught by a WHEN phrase: nonfatal -> RUNS; fatal -> DOES NOT RUN (abend at end of last handler); fatal but the raising statement carries a non-NOT conditional phrase (ON SIZE ERROR etc.) -> demoted by item 1 before item 4 is reached, WHEN is not even entered, FINALLY RUNS; fatal but the handler executes RESUME AT NEXT STATEMENT -> RUNS; fatal EC-I-O -> implementor latitude under item 3, a CONFORMANCE.md row.
(iii) exception matched by no WHEN phrase: nonfatal -> RUNS (14.6.13.1.4 items 3/4); fatal -> DOES NOT RUN (items 5/6/7).
(iv) EXIT PERFORM from imperative-statement-1 or any handler -> RUNS, skipping remaining handler phrases including WHEN COMMON (§14.9.14.4 GR4); EXIT PERFORM inside FINALLY -> lands after END-PERFORM (GR16); GO TO out of range / GOBACK / EXIT PROGRAM / STOP RUN / propagated exception -> DOES NOT RUN (no rule provides it; NOTE 9 contemplates exactly this and only advises against it).

THREE ADDITIONS to the adjudication, none of which change its conclusion:

1. GR18 is a normative defect and must be recorded as one. Its sentence 1 ('control is passed to the end of the PERFORM statement') is a superseded sentence left in place; its sentence 2 cross-references 'General rule 14.9.29', which is a clause number (RAISE), not a general rule. The intended text is 'General rule 20', matching GR17 and GR19 verbatim. Implement GR18 as GR20. This deserves a CONFORMANCE.md / spec-defect-log row, because a reader who stops at GR18 sentence 1 will emit FINALLY on the fatal-after-WHEN-OTHER path and be wrong.

2. RESUME AT NEXT STATEMENT in a WHEN phrase pre-empts WHEN COMMON, because RESUME is an unconditional transfer of control (§14.9.33.1) executed before GR19 can route to imperative-statement-4. The adjudication says RESUME reaches FINALLY but does not say WHEN COMMON is skipped. Annex D.16.5's second listing retains a WHEN COMMON block below a WHEN EC-SIZE containing RESUME, which is boilerplate carried from the first listing and should not be read as implying COMMON executes.

3. FINALLY executes with WHEN exception checking STILL ENABLED, because GR14 sites the implicit POP ALL / TURN OFF 'immediately preceding the END PERFORM phrase' — i.e. after imperative-statement-5, not before it. Combined with GR21 (an exception in imperative-statement-5 does not transfer to any of imperative-statement-2/3/4/5), this means an exception raised inside FINALLY is detected and enabled but handled by ordinary 14.6.13.1.3 machinery.
second.annexEvidence:
Annex D.16.5 'Inline exception processing' (specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 45643-45727) is decisive and I read both listings in full rather than trusting the packet. First listing, verbatim: the WHEN COMMON block closes with '>* exception fatal: run unit terminates' / '>* exception nonfatal: control is passed / >*   to **next statement**', and the FINALLY block drawn immediately below is annotated '*> come here for no matching exceptions / *> of if an EXIT PERFORM was in a WHEN'. FINALLY is not listed as a fatal-path destination despite sitting directly under the fatal-termination comment — a C# `finally` implementation would print the FINALLY text there. Crucially for the GR18 defect, this listing contains BOTH a WHEN OTHER and a WHEN COMMON, so the WHEN-OTHER fatal path demonstrably terminates rather than reaching FINALLY.

Second listing, introduced by 'You could avoid termination with something like this', adds RESUME AT NEXT STATEMENT to WHEN EC-SIZE and widens the FINALLY annotation to '*> come here for no matching exceptions / >* or a nonfatal was processed'. It closes with 'If you specified EXIT PERFORM in a WHEN, execution would proceed at FINALLY' — independent informative confirmation of §14.9.14.4 GR4 — and 'You are not allowed to do RESUME AT some-procedure', matching §14.9.33.3 SR1.

Two Annex D passages the adjudication under-used. The D.16.4 preamble (line 45620): 'Unless the exception occurs in a MERGE statement, a SORT statement, or an I-O statement for which the implementor specifies otherwise, one of the following occurs. 1) If the exception ... was a fatal exception, the run unit will be terminated if none of the above steps were taken.' — the informative echo of the 14.6.13.1.3 item 2/3 carve-outs, and it names RESUME and GOBACK RAISING as 'the above steps'. And the D.16.5 preamble (line 45643): 'Inline processing takes precedence over declarative processing when there is no specific phrase exception processing phrase (like SIZE ERROR) in the statement that caused the exception' — direct Annex support for the item-1 demotion, stronger than the ordering inference the adjudication offered.

Also confirmed: 'Some latitude is given to implementors to specify alternative treatment of fatal exceptions, in particular for input-output exceptions and for exception conditions that are not enabled' (line 45636), echoing item 3 and item 8.

No Annex E, Annex F, or docs/VERSION_CHANGE_REFERENCE.md entry alters any of this. The exception-checking PERFORM with FINALLY is 2023-only, so there is no prior-edition behavior to reconcile.
second.implementationConsequence:
The adjudication's implementation list (its items 1-9) is correct and I endorse it in full: emit imperative-statement-5 as PLAIN SEQUENTIAL CODE at the tail of the PERFORM — a labelled L_FINALLY block in the PC-dispatcher — NOT a C# `finally`/`try-finally`, which would be observably wrong on the fatal path and on transfer-out. Position-sensitive EXIT PERFORM lowering (goto L_FINALLY from imperative-statement-1 or any handler; goto L_AFTER_END_PERFORM from inside FINALLY). Honour the item-1 demotion upstream in the raise path — if the current C5 raise path branches on Table 13 fatality BEFORE checking for a handling non-NOT conditional phrase, that is a real defect. Honour RESUME AT NEXT STATEMENT pre-empting the item-4 abend.

FOUR ADDITIONS from this review:

A. GR18 must be implemented as GR20 (fatal after WHEN OTHER -> abend, NOT -> L_FINALLY), and the deviation from GR18's literal sentence 1 must be recorded as a spec-defect row in CONFORMANCE.md with the reasoning: sentence 2 supersedes sentence 1, and sentence 2's 'General rule 14.9.29' is a mis-substituted cross-reference for 'General rule 20' (cf. the verbatim-parallel GR17 and GR19). RESUME is an unconditional transfer of control; the dispatcher must set the PC to the statement after the raiser without routing through imperative-statement-4. Add a golden with WHEN EC-SIZE containing RESUME AT NEXT STATEMENT plus a WHEN COMMON that prints a marker: expect the COMMON marker ABSENT and the FINALLY marker PRESENT. This case is not in the adjudication's proposed golden list and is easy to get wrong, because Annex D.16.5's second listing still shows a WHEN COMMON block.

C. The implicit POP ALL / TURN OFF (GR14) must be emitted AFTER L_FINALLY, immediately before the END-PERFORM continuation point — not before FINALLY. Consequence: exceptions inside imperative-statement-5 are raised with the WHEN-enabled checking state still in effect, and are handled by ordinary 14.6.13.1.3 machinery with no FINALLY re-entry (GR21). Verify the current C5 emitter does not hoist the POP to the top of the tail block.

D. Extend the golden matrix beyond the adjudication's six with: (A) above, (B) above, and an EXIT PERFORM inside FINALLY landing after END-PERFORM (GR16's deliberate inversion). Keep the existing EC-BOUND-SUBSCRIPT golden (expect 'H','C', abend, neither 'F' nor 'AFTER') — I confirm it is correct, and it proves case (ii)-fatal. first.fork: C5-fork2-interior-TURN-legality — is a `>>TURN` directive legal INSIDE an exception-checking (format 3) PERFORM statement, given that §7.3.25.3 SR5 appears to forbid it while §14.9.28.4 GR14 specifies what it does?

governingText.quote: A TURN directive shall not be specified within an exception processing PERFORM statement.
governingText.bearing: The sole text alleged to forbid an interior >>TURN. Note its operative term is 'exception processing PERFORM statement' — a phrase that occurs EXACTLY ONCE in the entire normative text of the standard. Every other rule in the document that constrains constructs inside a format-3 PERFORM uses the term 'exception-checking PERFORM statement' (or 'exception checking PERFORM statement'). SR5 is the lone outlier.

governingText.quote: exception processing procedures\nprocedures within WHEN phrases within an exception-checking PERFORM statement or within a USE declarative
governingText.bearing: THE TIE-BREAKER. In the standard's own defined vocabulary, 'exception processing' does NOT name the format-3 PERFORM as a whole — it names specifically the WHEN-phrase handler code, and it is explicitly distinguished from 'exception-checking PERFORM statement', which appears as the containing construct in the same definition. SR5's phrase 'exception processing PERFORM statement' therefore reads as the exception-processing (handler) region of the PERFORM, not the whole statement. Had SR5 meant the whole statement it would have said 'exception-checking', as the POP and PUSH rules do verbatim.

governingText.quote: The POP directive shall not be specified within an exception checking PERFORM statement.
governingText.bearing: The genuinely flat, whole-statement prohibition, stated in the standard's standard vocabulary. Contrast with SR5's wording is deliberate-looking, not accidental.

governingText.quote: The PUSH directive shall not be specified within an exception checking PERFORM statement.
governingText.bearing: Same. PUSH/POP are banned across the entire format-3 PERFORM; TURN is not phrased the same way.

governingText.quote: Within imperative-statement-1 any TURN directive that turns off checking for an exception that is specified in a WHEN phrase will prevent that WHEN phrase from being invoked if that exception condition would otherwise have been set to exist.
governingText.bearing: DECISIVE, and it IS about a syntactically interior directive, not ambient state. 'imperative-statement-1' is a syntactic operand of the format-3 PERFORM; and per 7.3.25.1 a TURN directive 'is processed during the compilation stage of processing', so it cannot be 'within imperative-statement-1' in any runtime/ambient sense — only in the source text. This sentence assigns normative semantics to a >>TURN WRITTEN inside imperative-statement-1.

governingText.quote: An implicit PUSH ALL followed by TURN OFF ALL is assumed at the end of imperative-statement-1. Immediately preceding the END PERFORM phrase, there is an implicit POP ALL followed by an implicit TURN directive with OFF specified for any exception conditions that were implicitly turned on before the first statement in imperative-statement-1.
governingText.bearing: Supplies the STRUCTURAL reason the two regions are treated differently. The implicit PUSH ALL / TURN OFF ALL … POP ALL bracket spans exactly the handler region (imperative-statement-2/3/4/5). A user >>TURN written inside that bracket is unwound by the implicit POP ALL before END-PERFORM and has no defined lasting effect; a user >>TURN in imperative-statement-1 sits OUTSIDE the bracket and has a defined lasting effect (GR22). SR5 read as covering the handler region has real work to do and matches the mechanism; read as flat, it destroys GR14.

governingText.quote: If there is a TURN directive within the range of the PERFORM statement, the checking for that TURN directive is retained.
governingText.bearing: WEAKER THAN THE VERIFIER CLAIMED — it does NOT independently presuppose an interior TURN. 'Range' is a runtime notion defined in GR1 ('all those statements that are executed as a result of executing the PERFORM statement … Declarative procedures that are executed as a result … are included in the range'), so GR22 is satisfiable by a >>TURN in an out-of-line performed paragraph, entirely outside the PERFORM's own source text. It is consistent with an interior TURN but is not evidence for one. The verifier's '2-to-1' accounting is wrong on this point.

governingText.quote: The range of a PERFORM statement consists logically of all those statements that are executed as a result of executing the PERFORM statement through execution of the implicit transfer of control to the end of the PERFORM statement.
governingText.bearing: Defines 'range' as an execution-time notion, which is what disqualifies GR22 as evidence of syntactic interiority.

governingText.quote: checking for the exception condition associated with exception-name-1 is enabled for the procedure division statements and procedure division headers that follow in the compilation group
governingText.bearing: TURN's effect is purely LEXICAL over the compilation group. This is why GR14's sentence can only be about a directive lexically inside imperative-statement-1 — a TURN elsewhere could not selectively suppress a WHEN for statements inside imperative-statement-1.

governingText.quote: If specified within a statement, the TURN directive does not apply to any phrase of that statement. That TURN directive applies to any succeeding statement in the sequence of source lines, whether or not that succeeding statement is within the scope of the statement in which the TURN directive is specified.
governingText.bearing: Independently confirms that a TURN directive specified WITHIN a statement is a contemplated, well-defined construct generally, and fixes its scoping rule. Nothing here carves out PERFORM.

governingText.section: D.16.4 (informative — Annex D, Common exception processing)
governingText.quote: The use of PUSH and POP compiler directives allows manipulation of the TURN directives, but they shall not be specified within an exception-processing PERFORM statement.
governingText.bearing: CORROBORATING (informative). The annex restates the prohibition for PUSH and POP ONLY — 'they' refers to PUSH and POP — while in the same sentence describing TURN directives as the things being manipulated. The annex author's model is plainly: PUSH/POP banned inside a format-3 PERFORM; TURN not banned. No Annex D sentence anywhere states that TURN is banned inside a PERFORM.

governingText.quote: Inline exception processing. The PERFORM statement is enhanced to allow checking for exception conditions inline.
governingText.bearing: Confirms format-3 PERFORM is new in 2023, so SR5, GR14 and GR22 were all drafted together for this feature; the inconsistency is intra-edition drafting, with no prior-edition precedent to inherit.

first.derivation:
1. Establish what GR14 actually talks about — the prompt's central question. GR14 contains four sentences; they are NOT all about the same thing. Sentence 1 ("If checking … is not enabled for imperative-statement-1 by a TURN directive, an implicit TURN directive … is assumed") IS about ambient, outside-the-PERFORM checking state. But sentence 4 ("Within imperative-statement-1 any TURN directive that turns off checking …") is not: 'imperative-statement-1' is a syntactic operand, and §7.3.25.1 makes TURN a compile-stage construct that has no runtime existence to be "in effect within" anything. Combined with GR6/GR8 (TURN's effect is lexical over source order in the compilation group), a directive can only "prevent that WHEN phrase from being invoked" for statements that lexically follow it inside imperative-statement-1. GR14 sentence 4 therefore unambiguously describes a >>TURN WRITTEN INSIDE the PERFORM. The distinction the prompt asked me to police is real, and GR14 lands on the "written inside" side.

2. Demote GR22. GR22's "within the range of the PERFORM statement" uses 'range' as defined by GR1 — an execution-time notion that expressly includes out-of-line performed paragraphs and declarative procedures. A >>TURN in a paragraph PERFORMed from imperative-statement-1 is "within the range" without being written inside the statement. GR22 is consistent with, but does not presuppose, an interior TURN. The verifier's "2-to-1 for GR14" tally is therefore mis-counted: the real evidence is one dispositive normative sentence (GR14 s.4) plus one informative annex sentence (D.16.4), not two normative rules.

3. Read SR5's exact words, as instructed. SR5 does not say "shall not be specified within a format 3 PERFORM statement" and does not say "exception-CHECKING PERFORM statement". It says "within an exception PROCESSING PERFORM statement". That phrase appears exactly once in the normative text. Meanwhile §3.70 defines "exception processing procedures" as "procedures within WHEN phrases within an exception-checking PERFORM statement" — i.e. in this document's own controlled vocabulary, "exception processing" designates the WHEN-handler region and is explicitly contrasted with "exception-checking PERFORM statement" as the containing construct. The two sibling directive rules that DO impose a whole-statement ban (POP §7.3.20.3 SR4, PUSH §7.3.22.3 SR4) both use "exception checking PERFORM statement" verbatim. So SR5's prohibition, read in the standard's own terms, is the NARROWER one: no >>TURN within the exception-processing (WHEN / WHEN OTHER / WHEN COMMON / FINALLY) region of the PERFORM.

4. Confirm the narrow reading is mechanically motivated, not merely grammatically available. GR14 mandates "An implicit PUSH ALL followed by TURN OFF ALL … at the end of imperative-statement-1" and "Immediately preceding the END PERFORM phrase … an implicit POP ALL". That implicit save/restore bracket spans EXACTLY the handler region. A user >>TURN written inside the bracket is unwound by the implicit POP ALL before END-PERFORM and so has no defined surviving effect — precisely the sort of construct a syntax rule should forbid. A user >>TURN in imperative-statement-1 sits outside the bracket, and the standard tells you exactly what it does (GR14 s.4) and exactly what survives (GR22). The two regions are structurally different, and SR5 partitions them along that seam. Note also that the same bracket explains why PUSH/POP get the FLAT ban: an unbalanced user PUSH or POP anywhere in the statement would corrupt the compiler's implicit PUSH ALL/POP ALL pairing. The asymmetry between SR5's wording and PUSH/POP SR4's wording tracks a real asymmetry in the mechanism.

5. Apply the harmonization canon. Under the narrow reading, SR5, GR14 s.4, GR22, D.16.4, and §3.70 are ALL simultaneously true and all operative. Under the flat reading, GR14 sentence 4 becomes dead letter (semantics assigned to a construct that can never legally exist), GR22 sentence 2 loses its most natural referent, and D.16.4's PUSH/POP-only phrasing becomes a second error. A reading that renders one carefully drafted normative sentence nugatory and requires positing two further drafting errors is inferior to a reading under which every provision does work. The narrow reading wins.

6. Sanity check the direction of engineering risk. Even a reader who insists SR5 is flat must still implement GR14 s.4's semantics — a conforming compiler cannot both reject the construct and honor the rule that says what it does. So the ONLY behavioral divergence between the readings is whether to emit a diagnostic for a >>TURN in imperative-statement-1. Rejecting a program for which the standard supplies explicit semantics is the strictly worse error.
first.answer:
SPEC-RESOLVED. The premise that SR5 states a FLAT prohibition is false — SR5 states a NARROW one, and the sentence that resolves it is §3.70: "exception processing procedures — procedures within WHEN phrases within an exception-checking PERFORM statement or within a USE declarative."

SR5's operative term is "exception PROCESSING PERFORM statement", a phrase used exactly once in the normative text, whereas the two sibling whole-statement bans (POP §7.3.20.3 SR4, PUSH §7.3.22.3 SR4) both say "exception CHECKING PERFORM statement" verbatim. In this standard's own defined vocabulary, "exception processing" names the WHEN-handler region, expressly contrasted with "exception-checking PERFORM statement" as the containing construct. SR5 therefore forbids a >>TURN written in the handler region (imperative-statement-2/3/4/5 — WHEN, WHEN OTHER, WHEN COMMON, FINALLY), not one written in imperative-statement-1.

GR14 sentence 4 genuinely does describe a syntactically INTERIOR directive, not ambient state: "Within imperative-statement-1 any TURN directive that turns off checking for an exception that is specified in a WHEN phrase will prevent that WHEN phrase from being invoked." Since §7.3.25.1 makes TURN a compile-stage construct with no runtime existence, and GR6 makes its effect lexical over source order, "within imperative-statement-1" can only mean written there. The prompt's suspicion that GR14 might merely be about ambient checking state is correct for GR14 sentence 1 but wrong for sentence 4.

GR22 is NOT evidence, contrary to the verifier's "2-to-1" tally. Its "within the range of the PERFORM statement" uses 'range' as defined by GR1 — an execution-time notion that includes out-of-line performed paragraphs and declarative procedures — so GR22 is satisfiable without any interior TURN.

The partition is mechanically motivated, not merely a verbal escape: GR14 mandates an implicit PUSH ALL + TURN OFF ALL at the end of imperative-statement-1 and an implicit POP ALL immediately before END-PERFORM. That bracket spans exactly the handler region, so a >>TURN written inside it is unwound before the statement ends and has no defined surviving effect — exactly what a syntax rule should forbid. A >>TURN in imperative-statement-1 sits outside the bracket, and the standard specifies both its effect (GR14 s.4) and its survival (GR22). The same bracket explains why PUSH/POP get the flat ban: an unbalanced user PUSH/POP anywhere in the statement would corrupt the implicit pairing.

Answer: a >>TURN directive inside imperative-statement-1 of a format-3 PERFORM is LEGAL and has specified semantics; a >>TURN inside a WHEN / WHEN OTHER / WHEN COMMON / FINALLY handler is a SR5 violation. No owner decision is needed.

Honest caveat on confidence: this resolution is reached by harmonization plus a defined term, not by a single sentence that says "SR5 means the handler region". The wording of SR5 is a drafting defect and a reasonable reader could take it as flat. But that flat reading requires positing that GR14 s.4 is dead letter AND that D.16.4's PUSH/POP-only phrasing is a second error — and even then a conforming compiler must still implement GR14 s.4's semantics, so the only divergence is whether to also emit a diagnostic. The risk is one-sided.

second.classification: SPEC-RESOLVED — but resolved OPPOSITE to the adjudication under review on the legality question. SR5 is a FLAT, whole-statement prohibition. The adjudication's narrow-scope reading is refuted by the very Annex D sentence it cites.

governingText.quote: 5) A TURN directive shall not be specified within an exception processing PERFORM statement.
governingText.bearing: The prohibition. Grammatically, the head noun of 'an exception processing PERFORM statement' is 'PERFORM statement', with 'exception processing' as an attributive modifier and the indefinite article 'an' governing the whole. It names a KIND of statement, not a region within one. The adjudication's re-bracketing ('the exception-processing [region] of a PERFORM statement') is not available from this syntax — that meaning would require 'within the exception processing procedures of a PERFORM statement'.

governingText.quote: The use of PUSH and POP compiler directives allows manipulation of the TURN directives, but they shall not be specified within an exception-processing PERFORM statement.
governingText.bearing: THE ACTUAL TIE-BREAKER, AND IT CUTS AGAINST THE ADJUDICATION. The annex applies the phrase 'exception-processing PERFORM statement' to the PUSH/POP prohibition — whose normative statements (§7.3.20.3 SR4, §7.3.22.3 SR4) read 'exception checking PERFORM statement', and which the adjudication itself concedes is a FLAT whole-statement ban. So the drafters demonstrably use 'exception-processing PERFORM statement' and 'exception-checking PERFORM statement' as SYNONYMS naming the whole format-3 PERFORM. The adjudication quoted this exact sentence, mined it for the pronoun 'they', and missed that the phrase itself destroys its case. Grep confirms 'exception[- ]processing PERFORM' occurs exactly twice in the document: SR5 and here. One of the two is provably a synonym for the whole statement — so the phrase is not a term of art for the handler region.

governingText.quote:
exception processing procedures
procedures within WHEN phrases within an exception-checking PERFORM statement or within a USE declarative
governingText.bearing: THE ADJUDICATION'S CLAIMED TIE-BREAKER, OVER-READ. What §3.70 defines is the three-word term 'exception processing procedureS'. It does not define 'exception processing' as a standalone modifier meaning 'handler region', and SR5 does not use the defined term. The standard uses 'exception processing' loosely and broadly elsewhere — D.16.1 line 45572: 'There is more than one method of exception processing... The other method of exception processing is called common exception processing' — which is plainly the whole mechanism, not the WHEN region.

governingText.quote: If specified within a statement, the TURN directive does not apply to any phrase of that statement. That TURN directive applies to any succeeding statement in the sequence of source lines, whether or not that succeeding statement is within the scope of the statement in which the TURN directive is specified.
governingText.bearing: CORROBORATES THE FLAT READING, contrary to the adjudication's use of it. GR5 establishes 'specified within a statement' as the standard's own idiom for LEXICAL containment within a whole statement, scope-wide. SR5 uses that identical idiom — 'shall not be specified within an ... PERFORM statement'. Read against its sibling general rule, SR5 is a whole-statement lexical ban.

governingText.quote: Syntax rules supplement general formats, identify equivalent words, and define or clarify the order in which words or elements may be written to form larger elements such as phrases, clauses, or statements. Syntax rules may also impose restrictions on individual words or elements, relax restrictions implied by words or elements...
governingText.bearing: STRUCTURAL TIE-BREAKER THE ADJUDICATION NEVER LOOKED FOR. Syntax rules are the standard's instrument for what MAY BE WRITTEN. SR5 is a syntax rule.

governingText.quote: A general rule defines or clarifies the meaning or relationship of meanings of an element or set of elements. It is used to define or clarify the semantics of the statement and the effect that it has on either execution or compilation...
governingText.bearing: Completes the tie-break. GR14 is a GENERAL rule — it defines MEANING, not legality. A general rule cannot grant written-form permission that a syntax rule withholds. The adjudication treated GR14 s.4 as if it conferred legality; by §5.3.2/§5.3.3 it cannot.

governingText.section: 4.2.2 Acceptance of standard language elements — line 2395
governingText.quote: An implementation shall provide a warning mechanism that optionally may be invoked by the user at compile time to indicate violations of the general formats and the explicit syntax rules of standard COBOL.
governingText.bearing: DISSOLVES THE ADJUDICATION'S CENTRAL 'DEAD LETTER' ARGUMENT. Violations of explicit syntax rules need only be surfaced by a warning mechanism whose INVOCATION is at the user's option — a conforming implementation is not required to reject. governingText.quote: Within imperative-statement-1 any TURN directive that turns off checking for an exception that is specified in a WHEN phrase will prevent that WHEN phrase from being invoked if that exception condition would otherwise have been set to exist. governingText.bearing: Verified verbatim; the adjudication quoted it accurately. governingText.bearing: Verified verbatim. The adjudication treats the wording delta vs SR5 as deliberate. D.16.4 shows it is not — the annex restates THESE bans using SR5's phrase.

governingText.quote: If there is a TURN directive within the range of the PERFORM statement, the checking for that TURN directive is retained. / The range of a PERFORM statement consists logically of all those statements that are executed as a result of executing the PERFORM statement...

second.answer:
SPEC-RESOLVED, but the adjudication under review reaches the WRONG legality answer. I agree it is not an owner decision; I disagree on what to implement.

The adjudication's sole tie-breaker is that SR5's 'exception PROCESSING PERFORM statement' is a deliberate term of art meaning the WHEN-handler region, contrasted with the sibling rules' 'exception CHECKING PERFORM statement'. That is refuted by the very Annex D sentence the adjudication quotes. D.16.4 reads: 'The use of PUSH and POP compiler directives allows manipulation of the TURN directives, but they shall not be specified within an exception-processing PERFORM statement.' That sentence applies the phrase 'exception-processing PERFORM statement' to the PUSH/POP prohibition — stated normatively as 'exception checking PERFORM statement' and conceded by the adjudication to be FLAT. The phrase occurs exactly twice in the whole document (SR5 and D.16.4), and one of those two provably names the entire statement. It is a drafting synonym, not a term of art.

Three further points the adjudication missed, all pointing the same way. (1) TURN's own GR5 — 'If specified within a statement, the TURN directive does not apply to any phrase of that statement' — establishes 'specified within a statement' as the standard's idiom for whole-statement lexical containment; SR5 uses that idiom verbatim. (2) §5.3.2 makes syntax rules the instrument governing what 'may be written'; §5.3.3 makes general rules the instrument defining 'meaning'. GR14 is a general rule and cannot confer legality. (3) §4.2.2 requires only 'a warning mechanism that optionally may be invoked by the user' for syntax-rule violations — an implementation need not reject. That last point demolishes the adjudication's central harmonization argument: GR14 sentence 4 is NOT dead letter under the flat reading, because non-rejecting conforming compilers will accept an interior >>TURN and need a rule saying what it means. Every provision stays operative.

Grammar also matters: 'an exception processing PERFORM statement' has 'PERFORM statement' as its head noun under an indefinite article. It names a kind of statement. §3.70 defines the distinct three-word term 'exception processing procedureS', which SR5 does not use, and D.16.1 uses 'exception processing' expansively for the whole mechanism.

What I independently confirm from the adjudication: GR14 sentence 4 really does describe a syntactically interior directive (TURN is compile-stage per §7.3.25.1, its effect lexical per GR6/GR8, and GR14 sentence 1's implicit TURN ON forecloses an ambient reading); and GR22 is not evidence of interiority, since GR1 defines 'range' as execution-time including out-of-line paragraphs. Both were good catches.

adjudications.title: C6B: what LENGTH does a figurative constant have as the SUPPRESS WHEN suppression literal?

first.fork: C6B-figurative-length-GR2-vs-GR3 — when SUPPRESS WHEN literal-1 is a bare figurative constant (e.g. HIGH-VALUE) and the alternate key is fixed-length (say PIC X(4)), does §8.3.3.6.4 GR2 apply (figurative repeated to the key's length ⇒ 0xFF×4) or GR3b (length one ⇒ 0xFF compared to a 4-byte key, space-padded per §8.8.4.2.7(2) ⇒ 0xFF + 3 spaces)?

governingText.quote: Literal-1 establishes the key suppression value for this alternate record key for WRITE and REWRITE statements. Alternate record key suppression specifies that an alternate record key access path to a particular record shall not be provided when the value of data-name-1 or record-key-name-1 in that record is equal to literal-1.
governingText.bearing: Defines the operation as a comparison ('is equal to') between a named data item / record key and literal-1 — i.e. the figurative constant is *compared with* a data item.

governingText.quote: Literal-1 shall be an alphanumeric literal, a national literal, or a figurative constant, and shall be of the same category as data-name-1 or data-name-2. If ALL literal is specified, the literal shall be one character long.
governingText.bearing: Positively admits figuratives here (unlike the dozens of sites that say 'shall be neither a figurative constant nor a zero-length literal'), so the length question is live. The one-character restriction on ALL literal only makes sense if the figurative is replicated to the key length — under a length-one reading the restriction would be pointless.

governingText.quote: Data-name-1 and data-name-2 shall not reference a variable-length data item.
governingText.bearing: Guarantees the associated item is a FIXED-LENGTH data item — exactly the predicate GR2 names.

governingText.quote: When a figurative constant represents a string of one or more characters and the length of the string is specified in the rules for the context in which the figurative constant is used, then when this figurative constant is specified in a VALUE clause or in association with a fixed-length data item, literal, or intermediate result, the string of characters is repeated character by character until the size of the resultant string is greater than or equal to the number of character positions in the associated data item, literal, or intermediate result. This resultant string is then truncated from the right until the number of character positions remaining is equal either to 1 or to the number of character positions in the associated data item, literal, or intermediate result, whichever is greater.
governingText.bearing: The fill rule. Its trigger — association with a fixed-length data item — is satisfied here.

governingText.quote: A figurative constant is associated with a data item or literal when, for example, the figurative constant is moved to it, compared with it, or paired with it in a binary operation.
governingText.bearing: DISPOSITIVE. 'compared with it' is named explicitly as association. GR6's suppression test is precisely a comparison with data-name-1/record-key-name-1.

governingText.quote: When a figurative constant represents a string of one or more characters and the length of the string is not specified in the rules for the context in which the figurative constant is used, the length of the string is determined from context by applying the following rules in order: … b) When a figurative constant is other than ALL literal-1, the length of the string is one character. NOTE 2 For example, when the figurative constant appears in a DISPLAY, STOP, STRING, or UNSTRING statement, it is one character.
governingText.bearing: The residual rule, applicable only when GR2's predicate fails. Its NOTE 2 example set is characteristic of contexts with NO associated fixed-length receiver.

governingText.quote: The comparison used for determining changes to the key is based on the collating sequence for the file according to the rules for a relation condition.
governingText.bearing: Routes the suppression test through relation-condition semantics (§8.8.4.2.7) and fixes the collating sequence as the file's (per-key) sequence, not the program collating sequence.

governingText.quote: 2) Operands of unequal length. If the operands are of unequal length, comparison proceeds as though the shorter operand were extended on the right by sufficient alphanumeric spaces to make the operands of equal length.
governingText.bearing: Determines the (rejected) GR3b outcome: HIGH-VALUE would become 0xFF followed by three SPACES — the value actually tested would not be 'high values' at all.

governingText.section: 14.9.13 DISPLAY GR3 / STRING SR / UNSTRING GR (the NOTE 2 statements)
governingText.quote: If a figurative constant is specified as one of the operands, only a single occurrence of the figurative constant is displayed. … When a figurative constant is specified as literal-1 or literal-2, it refers to an implicit one character data item … When a figurative constant is used as the delimiter, it stands for a single-character national literal if identifier-1 is a national data item; otherwise, it stands for a single-character alphanumeric literal.
governingText.bearing: Confirms NOTE 2's example set is exactly the class of contexts where the figurative is a free-standing sending/delimiting operand with no associated fixed-length receiver. SUPPRESS WHEN is not in that class.

governingText.quote: The figurative constant SPACE when specified in the REWRITE statement references one alphanumeric space character.
governingText.bearing: Structural proof the committee writes an EXPLICIT length-one override whenever it wants one despite an associated item. §12.4.5.6 contains no such override — so the GR2 default stands.

governingText.quote: A figurative constant may be used whenever 'literal' appears in a format or when a rule allows it, with the following restrictions: … b) A figurative constant shall not be specified where a syntax rule prohibits it.
governingText.bearing: The permission rule for figuratives. Relevant to whether §13.18.40 SR9 actually REJECTS figuratives in the EDITING phrase (see answer — the brief's premise is not fully supportable).

governingText.quote: literal-1, literal-2, and literal-3 shall be national literals. Otherwise, literal-1, literal-2, and literal-3 shall be alphanumeric literals. The total number of characters in literal-1, literal-2, or literal-3 shall not exceed 50. … If character-1 is a simple insertion symbol or a fixed insertion symbol, the size of literal-1 is counted in the size of the item.
governingText.bearing: In the EDITING phrase the length flows FROM the literal TO the item — the item's size is DERIVED from the literal's size. There is therefore no antecedent associated length for GR2 to fill to, so GR3b (length one) governs regardless of the SR9 permission question.

first.derivation:
1. GR2 and GR3 are mutually exclusive by construction: GR3's protasis is the negation of GR2's ("the length of the string is NOT specified in the rules for the context"). So the only real question is whether GR2's predicate is satisfied.

2. GR2's predicate has two conjuncts, and the second one is the operative discriminator: the figurative must be "specified in a VALUE clause or in association with a fixed-length data item, literal, or intermediate result." NOTE 1 defines "association" and lists three exemplars, the second of which is "compared with it."

3. §12.4.5.6.4 GR6 states the suppression test as "the value of data-name-1 or record-key-name-1 in that record is equal to literal-1" — a comparison of the figurative with a data item. GR24 confirms it is a relation-condition comparison. So literal-1 IS "compared with" data-name-1/record-key-name-1 ⇒ associated, per NOTE 1.

4. That associated item is fixed-length by SR3 ("shall not reference a variable-length data item"), and for record-key-name-1 the length is the concatenation of all data-name-2 occurrences (GR2 of §12.4.5.6.4). So "fixed-length data item" is satisfied literally and unambiguously. GR2's first conjunct is then also satisfied: the context rules DO fix the length, because the comparison is against an item of known fixed size — which is what "the length of the string is specified in the rules for the context" means (the context supplies the length; GR2 supplies the algorithm for producing a string of that length). If read otherwise, GR2's second conjunct and NOTE 1 would be dead text: every case GR2 describes (VALUE clause, move, comparison, binary operation) is a case where the length comes from an associated item, and no other class of context exists in which a length is "specified by the rules of the context."

5. Cross-check on NOTE 2: DISPLAY, STOP, STRING, UNSTRING are all contexts in which the figurative is a free-standing sending or delimiting operand with no fixed-length receiver sizing it — DISPLAY has a device, STOP a message, STRING/UNSTRING a delimiter matched against a stream. Each of those statements separately states length one in its own General/Syntax rules. So YES: NOTE 2's example set is characteristic of contexts LACKING an associated fixed-length receiver, and SUPPRESS WHEN is categorically unlike them.

6. Structural cross-check: where the committee wants length one DESPITE an associated fixed-length item, it says so in the statement's own rules — REWRITE GR8 and WRITE GR6 ("The figurative constant SPACE … references one alphanumeric space character"). §12.4.5.6 contains no such override, so the GR2 default is the intended reading.

7. Cross-check via SR7's own text: "If ALL literal is specified, the literal shall be one character long." Under the GR3 reading, ALL literal-1's length would be the length of literal-1 (GR3c) = one, and the key comparison would then be one character + space padding — making the one-character restriction gratuitous and actively harmful. Under GR2 the restriction is exactly right: a one-character ALL literal replicates cleanly to any key length. SR7 is only coherent under GR2.

8. Reductio on GR3b: with a PIC X(4) key, GR3b + §8.8.4.2.7(2) yields a suppression value of 0xFF followed by three SPACE characters. That is not "high values" in any sense a programmer or the Annex D description ("allows suppression of records that match a literal") would recognize, and it would make SUPPRESS WHEN HIGH-VALUE unable to suppress an all-0xFF key — the canonical use. No rule supports that outcome; it arises only from mis-selecting GR3.

9. On the C4 side-question, I cannot fully confirm the brief's premise. §13.18.40.3 SR9 constrains the CLASS of literal-1/2/3 ("shall be national literals … otherwise … alphanumeric literals") but does not contain the explicit exclusion the standard uses everywhere it means to bar figuratives ("shall be neither a figurative constant nor a zero-length literal" — §13.x ×6, §12.4.5.x, §14.x). Under §8.3.3.6.3 SR1, a figurative "may be used whenever 'literal' appears in a format … [unless] a syntax rule prohibits it," and literal-1 does appear in the Format 1 diagram; §8.3.3.6.4 GR1 gives figuratives an alphanumeric or national character value, so a class constraint alone does not obviously exclude them. The counter-evidence is that §8.3.3 enumerates "figurative constant values" (8.3.3.6) as a peer kind alongside "alphanumeric literals" (8.3.3.2, defined by its quoted/hex general formats), and §12.4.5.6.3 SR7 itself lists "an alphanumeric literal, a national literal, or a figurative constant" as three alternatives — i.e. the standard's own taxonomy treats a figurative as not being an alphanumeric literal. That reading supports the reject. Either way, C4 has no figurative-LENGTH question: in the EDITING phrase the size flows from the literal to the item ("the size of literal-1 is counted in the size of the item"), so there is no antecedent associated length for GR2 to fill to, and GR3b gives one character.
first.answer:
SPEC-RESOLVED in favor of GR2 (fill to key length). The sentence that resolves it is NOTE 1 to §8.3.3.6.4 GR2: "A figurative constant is associated with a data item or literal when, for example, the figurative constant is moved to it, COMPARED WITH IT, or paired with it in a binary operation" — read together with §12.4.5.6.4 GR6, which frames suppression as "the value of data-name-1 or record-key-name-1 in that record is equal to literal-1," and §12.4.5.6.3 SR3, which guarantees that item is fixed-length. GR2's predicate is therefore satisfied on its face, and GR3 (whose protasis is GR2's negation) is inapplicable.

Concretely: SUPPRESS WHEN HIGH-VALUE against a PIC X(4) alternate key means the suppression value is 0xFF repeated 4 times, and the runtime comparison is an EQUAL-LENGTH comparison per §8.8.4.2.7(1). The 0xFF-once-plus-space-padding outcome is wrong and never occurs — no space padding can ever arise, because GR2 makes the operands equal-length by construction.

Additionally, on the C4 companion claim: I can confirm C4 has no figurative-length question, but NOT for the reason the brief gives. §13.18.40.3 SR9 is a class constraint, not one of the standard's explicit figurative prohibitions ("shall be neither a figurative constant nor…"), and §8.3.3.6.3 SR1 permits figuratives wherever 'literal' appears in a format absent a prohibiting syntax rule. The reject is defensible on the taxonomy argument (§8.3.3 enumerates figurative constants as a peer kind to alphanumeric literals, and §12.4.5.6.3 SR7 lists the three as alternatives), but it is an inference, not a quoted prohibition — the diagnostic should be justified on that taxonomy basis, and it is worth flagging as a lower-confidence rejection than the brief assumes. Independently, even if a figurative were admitted in the EDITING phrase, §13.18.40.5 makes the ITEM's size derive from the LITERAL's size, so there is no associated length for GR2 to fill to and GR3b yields one character. Either path, C4 needs no owner decision.
first.annexEvidence: Annex D (informative), at the alternate-key discussion: "The SUPPRESS WHEN phrase when specified in the ALTERNATE RECORD KEY clause allows suppression of records that MATCH A LITERAL. When using that alternate key to access the file, the records suppressed would be skipped on reading the file and ignored when using the START statement." — "match a literal" describes a whole-key match, consistent with GR2 fill and inconsistent with a one-byte-plus-spaces test. Annex E substantive-change list item 42: "The SUPPRESS WHEN phrase may be specified as part of the ALTERNATE RECORD KEY clause to suppress access to a record via a particular alternate record key when THE VALUE OF THIS KEY EQUALS THE VALUE specified in this phrase" — again a value-of-the-whole-key equality, and it confirms SUPPRESS WHEN is new in 2023 (so there is no prior-edition practice to fork against; VERSION_CHANGE_REFERENCE should carry it as 2023-introduced with no 85/2002/2014 behavior). No Annex D worked example shows a figurative used as literal-1, so neither annex contradicts GR2; both corroborate it.
first.implementationConsequence:
Binder (ALTERNATE RECORD KEY clause):
1. SR7 gate (unchanged): literal-1 must be alphanumeric literal, national literal, or figurative constant, same category as data-name-1/data-name-2; if ALL literal, diagnose unless the literal is exactly one character.
2. NEW — figurative expansion at bind time. Compute keyLen = the fixed size of data-name-1, or for record-key-name-1 the sum of the sizes of all data-name-2 occurrences in SOURCE order (§12.4.5.6.4 GR2). SR3 guarantees this is a compile-time constant. Then apply §8.3.3.6.4 GR2 verbatim: repeat the figurative's character value until length >= keyLen, then truncate from the right to max(1, keyLen) — with keyLen >= 1 always, this is simply "replicate to exactly keyLen." Units are alphanumeric character positions for an alphanumeric key and NATIONAL character positions for a national key (§8.3.3.6.4 GR1 selects the national representation when the context requires national characters; §12.4.5.6.3 SR2/SR7 fix the category). Do NOT emit a length-1 constant and rely on comparison padding.
3. ALL literal-1 takes the same path: the one-character literal replicates to keyLen.
4. HIGH-VALUE / LOW-VALUE must NOT be frozen to 0xFF/0x00 at bind time as a semantic commitment: §8.3.3.6.4 GR6/GR7 say that outside SPECIAL-NAMES the value at runtime is the highest/lowest ordinal position in the RUNTIME collating sequence (and the locale's LC_COLLATE sequence when in effect). Emit the replicated suppression value as a runtime-resolved constant of length keyLen, resolved once at file-open/first-use against the effective sequence.

Runtime (WRITE and REWRITE only — never READ/START, which merely observe the resulting index per the GR6 NOTE):
5. On WRITE, and on REWRITE for each alternate key, compare the current key value against the replicated suppression value. Use §8.8.4.2.7(1) equal-length comparison — operands are equal-length by construction, so the padding branch §8.8.4.2.7(2) is unreachable and should be an assert, not a code path.
6. The collating sequence is the FILE's (per-key, per §12.4.5.7 COLLATING SEQUENCE clause), not the program collating sequence — §12.4.5.6.4 GR24: "based on the collating sequence for the file according to the rules for a relation condition."
7. REWRITE transition handling per GR24: value now equals suppression value ⇒ drop the access path and reposition so the record is not found via this key; value no longer equals it ⇒ (re)provide the path and position it to be found. Suppressed entries never raise a duplicate-key condition and never require DUPLICATES.

The GR3b reading additionally produces an outcome (0xFF + spaces) that no rule or annex supports. I would not spend an owner decision on this. governingText.quote: When a figurative constant represents a string of one or more characters and the length of the string is specified in the rules for the context in which the figurative constant is used, then when this figurative constant is specified in a VALUE clause or in association with a fixed-length data item, literal, or intermediate result, the string of characters is repeated character by character until the size of the resultant string is greater than or equal to the number of character positions in the associated data item, literal, or intermediate result. governingText.bearing: The fill rule. (The packet truncated the final JUSTIFIED sentence — harmless here.) Its second conjunct, association with a fixed-length data item, is the operative discriminator.

governingText.section: 8.3.3.6.4 GR2, NOTE 1 (verified verbatim, immediately under GR2 and BEFORE GR3)
governingText.quote: A figurative constant is associated with a data item or literal when, for example, the figurative constant is moved to it, compared with it, or paired with it in a binary operation.
governingText.bearing: Decisive. Its physical placement under GR2 — not GR3 — means moves and COMPARISONS are GR2 contexts by the standard's own construction.

governingText.section: 14.9.25 MOVE statement (the rule set for the archetypal association) — I searched the entire MOVE section for any length rule for figuratives; there is none. GR at the fixed-point sizing rule reads:
governingText.quote: If the sending operand is a figurative constant, the number of digits is the same as the number of digits in the receiving operand and the figurative constant is replicated in this item, from left to right, as described in the rules for figurative constants.
governingText.bearing: MY INDEPENDENT KILL-SHOT for the strict counter-reading. MOVE contains NO statement-local rule specifying a figurative's length; it defers entirely to 8.3.3.6.4. Therefore 'the length of the string is specified in the rules for the context' in GR2 CANNOT mean 'an explicit per-statement length rule exists' — if it did, MOVE SPACES TO PIC X(4) would fall to GR3b and yield one space, and MOVE HIGH-VALUES TO PIC X(4) would yield 0xFF+3 spaces.
